📽️ Revision slideshow: Acids, Bases & Salts

1. Acids, bases and neutral substances

AcidsBases (alkalis)
TasteSour (lemon, vinegar)Bitter (baking soda, soap)
FeelCan sting skinSoapy / slippery
Blue litmusTurns redStays blue
Red litmusStays redTurns blue
pHLess than 7More than 7
Natural examplesCitric acid (lemons, oranges), acetic acid (vinegar), lactic acid (curd), tartaric acid (tamarind), formic acid (ant sting), oxalic acid (spinach)Baking soda, soap, toothpaste, lime water (calcium hydroxide), milk of magnesia
Lab examplesHydrochloric acid (HCl), sulphuric acid, nitric acidSodium hydroxide (NaOH), calcium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide

A base is any substance that neutralises an acid. A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali. Neutral substances, like pure water, salt solution and sugar solution, are neither acidic nor basic.

Safety: Never taste or touch lab chemicals to test them. Strong acids and strong bases are both corrosive: they burn skin. Use indicators instead. When diluting an acid, always add acid to water, slowly, never water to acid.

2. Indicators and the pH scale

An indicator is a substance that changes colour in an acid or a base.

IndicatorIn acidIn baseIn neutral
Litmus (from lichens)Blue → redRed → blueNo change
TurmericStays yellowRed / reddish-brownYellow
China rose (hibiscus)Dark pink / magentaGreenNo change
PhenolphthaleinColourlessPinkColourless
Universal indicatorShows a range of colours; compare with a chart to read the pH number
  • The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. pH 7 = neutral.
  • Below 7 = acidic. The lower the number, the stronger the acid (pH 1 is much stronger than pH 5).
  • Above 7 = alkaline. The higher the number, the stronger the alkali.
  • Litmus only tells you acid or base. Universal indicator also tells you how strong.
Reading results: A solution turns universal indicator dark green-blue, about pH 9. It is a weak alkali, like baking soda solution. Blue litmus would stay blue; red litmus would turn blue; phenolphthalein would turn pink.

3. Neutralisation

Acid + Base → Salt + Water (+ heat)
Hydrochloric acid + Sodium hydroxide → Sodium chloride + Water

When an acid and a base react, they cancel out each other's effects. This is neutralisation. Heat is given out, so the mixture gets warm. Adding a base to an acid little by little raises the pH towards 7. Adding an acid to a base lowers it towards 7.

Neutralisation in daily life

SituationProblemFix (and why)
IndigestionToo much hydrochloric acid in the stomachTake an antacid (e.g. milk of magnesia), a mild base
Ant / bee stingFormic acid injected into skinRub on baking soda (a mild base) or calamine
Wasp stingAlkaline stingUse a mild acid like vinegar
Acidic soilToo much chemical fertiliser; crops grow badlyAdd quicklime / slaked lime (bases)
Basic soilToo alkalineAdd organic matter (compost), which releases acids
Factory wasteAcidic waste kills fish in riversNeutralise it with a base before releasing it
Tooth decayBacteria make acids from sugar, which dissolve enamelBrush with toothpaste (basic)
The swimming pool question: A pool's pH falls from 7.2 to 6.1 after two days of rain. Why? Rainwater is slightly acidic: carbon dioxide (and pollution gases) dissolve in it. Lots of rain made the pool more acidic. Fix: add a mild base such as sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda) or soda ash a little at a time. It neutralises the extra acid. Keep testing with a pH kit until it is back near 7.2.

Acid rain: gases like sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide from factories and vehicles dissolve in rain, making it more acidic (pH below about 5.6). It damages buildings (the marble of the Taj Mahal), forests and lakes.

✅ Quick check: Acids & Bases

1. A liquid turns turmeric red and phenolphthalein pink. Is it acidic, basic or neutral?

Basic. Both indicators change colour only in a base.

2. Which is the stronger acid: pH 2 or pH 5? Explain.

pH 2. The lower the pH, the stronger the acid.

3. Why do farmers add lime to some fields?

The soil is too acidic. Lime is a base that neutralises the acid and raises the pH so crops grow well.

4. Why does the mixture get warm when an acid is neutralised by a base?

Neutralisation gives out heat.

📽️ Revision slideshow: Light

1. How light behaves

  • Light is a form of energy that lets us see. Objects that give out their own light (the Sun, a bulb, a candle) are luminous. Most objects (the Moon, a book) are non-luminous: we see them because they reflect light into our eyes.
  • Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation) and is very fast: about 3 lakh km per second.
  • A ray is the path of light shown as a line with an arrow. A beam is a bundle of rays.

2. Reflection and its laws

Reflection is the bouncing back of light when it hits a surface. Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors give regular reflection, so you see a clear image. Rough surfaces like paper scatter light in all directions, giving irregular (diffused) reflection, so there is no image.

  • Normal: an imaginary line at 90° to the mirror at the point where the ray hits.
  • Angle of incidence (i): between the incident ray and the normal. Angle of reflection (r): between the reflected ray and the normal.
  • Law 1: ∠i = ∠r. Law 2: The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.
Common trap: If a ray makes 30° with the mirror, the angle of incidence is 90 − 30 = 60°, not 30°. A ray hitting the mirror along the normal (i = 0°) bounces straight back.

3. Images in a plane mirror

  • Lateral inversion means the left and right sides are swapped. Your right hand appears as the image's left hand.
  • If you stand 2 m in front of a mirror, your image is 2 m behind it, so it is 4 m from you. If you walk 1 m towards the mirror, the distance between you and your image shrinks by 2 m.
  • Uses: dressing mirror, periscope (two mirrors at 45° let submarine crews see above water), kaleidoscope (mirrors at angles make repeating patterns).

4. Spherical mirrors, lenses and colours

TypeShapeEffect on lightImage & uses
Concave mirrorCurved inwards (like the inside of a spoon)Converges (brings together)Can form real, inverted images or enlarged upright images. Torch and headlight reflectors, shaving and dentist's mirrors, solar cookers.
Convex mirrorCurved outwards (back of a spoon)Diverges (spreads out)Always virtual, upright, smaller, and shows a wide area. Car side and rear-view mirrors, shop security mirrors.
Convex lensThicker in the middleConvergesMagnifying glass, camera, microscope, correcting long sight
Concave lensThinner in the middleDivergesAlways smaller, upright images. Correcting short sight.

White light is a mixture of seven colours: VIBGYOR (violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red). A prism splits them (dispersion). Raindrops do the same and make a rainbow, which is why you see rainbows when the Sun is behind you after rain. A spinning Newton's disc painted with the seven colours looks white, which proves it.

5. The pinhole camera

A pinhole camera is a closed box with a tiny hole on one side and a screen (tracing paper) on the other. Light from an object passes through the hole and forms an image on the screen. It works only because light travels in straight lines.

Why is the image upside down?

Light from the top of the object travels in a straight line through the hole and lands at the bottom of the screen. Light from the bottom lands at the top. The rays cross at the pinhole, so the image is inverted (and left–right swapped too).

Feature of the imagePinhole camera
Upright or upside down?Inverted (upside down)
Can it be caught on a screen?Yes — it forms on the tracing paper
ColoursSame colours as the object
SizeUsually smaller; it gets bigger if the screen is moved further from the pinhole

Make a sliding pinhole camera (Activity 11.10)

  1. Take two boxes that slide one inside the other.
  2. Make a pinhole in the middle of one face of the larger box.
  3. Cut a window in the smaller box and cover it with tracing paper (the screen).
  4. Slide the small box in, tracing-paper side inside.
  5. Point the pinhole at a bright, distant object; cover your head and the open end with a dark cloth.
  6. Slide the small box in or out until the image is sharp.
Pinhole camera vs plane mirrorPinhole cameraPlane mirror
ImageInvertedErect (upright)
On a screen?YesNo
Left–rightSwappedSwapped (lateral inversion)
Exam tips: draw the rays with a ruler as straight lines that cross at the pinhole; draw the image upside down; label object, pinhole, screen, inverted image. Never point a pinhole camera at the Sun. A bigger hole gives a brighter but blurred image; a small hole gives a sharper one.
Q: Why do we cover our head with a dark cloth when using a pinhole camera?

To block extra light, so the faint image on the tracing paper is easy to see.

Q: What does the pinhole camera prove about light?

That light travels in straight lines — that is why the rays cross at the hole and the image is inverted.

Q: How can you make the image larger?

Slide the screen further away from the pinhole (pull the inner box out).

✅ Quick check: Light

1. A ray strikes a mirror at 25° to its surface. What is the angle of reflection?

Angle of incidence = 90 − 25 = 65°, so the angle of reflection = 65°.

2. Why is AMBULANCE written backwards on the front of ambulances?

Because of lateral inversion. Drivers ahead see it the right way round in their mirrors.

3. Why are convex mirrors used as car side mirrors?

They always give an upright image and show a much wider field of view.

4. Can you see a book in a completely dark room? Explain.

No. The book is non-luminous. We see it only when light reflects off it into our eyes.

📽️ Revision slideshow: Shadows

1. How shadows form

A shadow is a dark area formed when an opaque object blocks light. Because light travels in straight lines, it can't bend around the object. You need three things: a light source, an opaque object, and a screen (a wall or the ground) to see it on.

  • A shadow is always on the opposite side of the object from the light.
  • A shadow is always black/dark, whatever the colour of the object. It shows the object's outline (shape) only, not its colour or details.
  • Transparent objects make almost no shadow. Translucent objects make a faint shadow.

2. What changes the size of a shadow?

ChangeEffect on shadow
Move the object closer to the lightShadow gets bigger (and more blurred at the edges)
Move the object closer to the screenShadow gets smaller and sharper
Move the light higher above the objectShadow gets shorter
Make the light source largerFuzzy edges appear (a partial shadow)

3. Shadows from the Sun

  • In the morning the Sun is low in the east, so shadows are long and point west.
  • At noon the Sun is highest, so shadows are shortest.
  • In the evening the Sun is low in the west, so shadows are long and point east.
  • A sundial uses the moving shadow of a stick to tell the time.
  • Eclipses are giant shadows. In a solar eclipse the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and its shadow falls on Earth. In a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

4. Pinhole camera

Light from the top of the object travels in a straight line through the tiny hole to the bottom of the screen, and light from the bottom goes to the top. So the image is inverted. This is more proof that light travels in straight lines. A bigger hole makes the image brighter but blurrier.

✅ Quick check: Shadows

1. A red ball and a blue ball of the same size are held in front of a torch. Describe their shadows.

Both shadows are dark and circular, the same size if at the same distance. A shadow never shows colour.

2. At 4 pm your shadow points east. Where is the Sun?

In the west. The shadow is on the opposite side of the light.

3. In a shadow investigation, what is the independent variable if you change the lamp's distance and measure the shadow's height?

The lamp distance (it's what you change). The shadow height is the dependent variable.

📽️ Revision slideshow: Electricity

1. Electric circuits

Electric current is the flow of electric charge. It can only flow around a complete, closed path called a circuit. A cell supplies the energy. Current flows from the positive (+) terminal, through the wires and components, back to the negative (−) terminal.

  • Closed circuit: complete path, so current flows and the bulb lights. Open circuit: a gap anywhere, so no current flows.
  • A switch opens or closes the circuit. It doesn't make electricity; it just completes or breaks the path.
  • Conductors let current pass: metals like copper, aluminium and iron, plus graphite and impure water. Insulators don't: plastic, rubber, wood, glass, dry air. Wires are copper (a good conductor) covered in plastic (an insulator) for safety.

Scientists draw circuits with symbols in a circuit diagram: straight lines for wires, drawn as a neat rectangle. In a cell symbol, the longer thin line is + and the shorter thick line is −.

Why doesn't the bulb light? (Troubleshooting)

  1. Is the switch closed?
  2. Is the cell flat, or connected the wrong way in a battery (+ must join −)?
  3. Is the bulb fused (broken filament)?
  4. Is any wire loose or broken?

Test one thing at a time by swapping that part for one you know works.

2. Heating effect of electric current

ℹ️ Not in the new Curiosity Ch 3 — extra knowledge; check with your teacher if it's in your exam.

  • When current flows through a wire, the wire gets hot. How hot depends on the material, length and thickness of the wire, and on the current.
  • A bulb's thin tungsten filament gets so hot (over 2,000 °C) that it glows. Much of the energy is wasted as heat, which is why LEDs and CFLs are more efficient.
  • Fuse: a thin wire that melts when too much current flows (a short circuit or overload), breaking the circuit and preventing fires. MCBs (miniature circuit breakers) do the same job and can be switched back on.
  • Always use ISI-marked appliances and never touch switches with wet hands.

3. Magnetic effect of electric current

ℹ️ Not in the new Curiosity Ch 3 — extra knowledge; check with your teacher if it's in your exam.

A wire carrying current behaves like a magnet. It deflects a compass needle placed near it (discovered by Hans Christian Oersted). Coil insulated wire around an iron nail and pass current through it, and you get an electromagnet. It is a magnet only while current flows. That's its big advantage: it can be switched on and off.

Electric bell: pressing the switch makes the electromagnet attract an iron strip with a hammer, which hits the gong. This breaks the circuit, so the magnet switches off and the strip springs back, which completes the circuit again. The cycle repeats very fast, so the bell rings continuously.

✅ Quick check: Electricity

1. In a series circuit with two bulbs, one bulb fuses. What happens and why?

Both go out. There is only one path, so the gap stops current everywhere.

2. Why are house lights wired in parallel?

Each light has its own path, so you can switch them separately, and if one fails the others still work.

3. Why is a fuse wire made thin with a low melting point?

So it heats up and melts quickly when the current is too high, breaking the circuit before wires overheat and cause a fire.

4. Give two ways to make an electromagnet stronger.

More turns of wire; more cells (bigger current); use a soft-iron core.

📽️ Revision slideshow: Digestion

1. Nutrition in humans

Humans take in food in five steps: ingestion (taking food in), digestion (breaking it into small, soluble substances), absorption (into the blood), assimilation (body cells using it to build and get energy) and egestion (removing undigested waste).

Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces (chewing, churning), which increases its surface area. Chemical digestion uses enzymes in digestive juices to break big molecules into small ones: starch → glucose, proteins → amino acids, fats → fatty acids and glycerol.

The alimentary canal is a long tube from the mouth to the anus: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus. The liver, gall bladder and pancreas are glands that add juices but food does not pass through them.

2. Organ by organ

OrganWhat happens
Mouth (buccal cavity)Teeth cut and grind food. The tongue mixes it with saliva, which contains an enzyme that begins turning starch into sugar. (Chew a piece of roti for a long time and it tastes sweet!) The tongue also tastes food and helps swallow.
Oesophagus (food pipe)Pushes food down by waves of muscle contraction called peristalsis. No digestion happens here.
StomachA thick-walled muscular bag that churns food. Its lining releases hydrochloric acid (kills bacteria, makes the stomach acidic), digestive juices that start protein digestion, and mucus that protects the lining from the acid.
LiverThe largest gland. It makes bile, stored in the gall bladder. Bile neutralises the acid from the stomach and breaks fats into tiny droplets.
PancreasMakes pancreatic juice, which is basic (neutralises acid) and digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Small intestineThe longest part: almost 6 m long (about twice the height of a classroom) and highly coiled. Digestion is completed here, and digested food is absorbed through millions of villi into the blood.
Large intestineAbout 1.5 m, shorter but wider. Absorbs water and some salts from the undigested food.
Rectum and anusThe rectum stores the waste (faeces). It is removed through the anus (egestion).

3. Keeping your gut healthy

  • Diarrhoea (watery stools, often from infection) can cause dangerous loss of water and salts (dehydration). First aid is ORS (oral rehydration solution: boiled cooled water + sugar + salt).
  • Fibre (roughage) from vegetables, fruit and whole grains isn't digested, but it helps food move and prevents constipation.

🦷 Teeth types and tooth decay are now in the Extra: Teeth tab (not for the exam).

3b. Testing food: the iodine test for starch

Iodine solution is brownish-yellow. When you put a few drops on a food that contains starch, it turns BLUE-BLACK. If there is no starch, it stays brownish-yellow.

Activity: what does saliva do to starch?

  • Plate A: some plain boiled rice. Plate B: boiled rice that has been chewed for 3–5 minutes (mixed with saliva).
  • Add 2–3 drops of dilute iodine solution to each.
  • A turns blue-black: it still has starch. B shows little or no blue-black: the enzyme in saliva (salivary amylase) has broken the starch down into sugar.
  • That is why chewed roti or rice starts to taste sweet.

Activity: saliva in test tubes

  • Two test tubes with rice flour (or starch) mixed in water. Add saliva to tube B only; tube A is the control.
  • Wait 35–45 minutes, then add iodine to both.
  • Tube A turns blue-black (starch still there). Tube B does not, or only slightly (saliva digested the starch).
Food tested with iodineColourWhy
Chapati / roti, bread, boiled riceBlue-blackMade from grains: rich in starch
Boiled potatoBlue-blackPotato is rich in starch
Chewed chapati or riceLittle or no changeSaliva has changed starch to sugar
Sugar, salt, oil, egg white, cucumberStays brownish-yellowNo (or very little) starch

Other food tests (recap)

NutrientTestPositive result
StarchAdd iodine solutionTurns blue-black
ProteinAdd copper sulphate solution + caustic soda (sodium hydroxide)Turns violet / purple
FatRub the food on paper and hold it to the lightAn oily, see-through (translucent) patch

4. Digestion in other animals (quick view)

  • Grass-eaters (ruminants) such as cows, goats and buffaloes swallow grass quickly into the rumen (first part of the stomach), where it is partly digested (cud). Later they bring it back to the mouth and chew the cud (rumination). Bacteria in the rumen digest cellulose, which humans can't.
  • Birds have no teeth. They swallow small stones that stay in a muscular part of the stomach called the gizzard, which grinds the food.
  • Amoeba (single-celled) traps food with pseudopodia ("false feet") in a food vacuole and digests it there.

✅ Quick check: Digestion

1. Where is digestion completed and where is most food absorbed?

Both in the small intestine (absorption through the villi).

2. How are villi adapted for absorption?

Millions of finger-like folds give a huge surface area; thin walls; a rich supply of blood capillaries.

3. Why doesn't the stomach digest itself?

Its lining releases mucus, which protects it from the acid and digestive juices.

4. What is the function of bile? Where is it made and stored?

It breaks fats into small droplets for easier digestion. It is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

📽️ Revision slideshow: Breathing & Respiration

1. Life processes in animals

Life processes are the activities that go on all the time to keep an animal alive: getting food and digesting it, breathing in oxygen, respiration (releasing energy from food), transporting substances around the body, and removing waste. (Digestion is in the 🍎 Digestion tab; this tab covers breathing, respiration, circulation and excretion.)

Why do we need oxygen? Every cell needs energy to work. Cells get it by breaking down digested food (glucose) using oxygen. Carbon dioxide is made as a waste product and must be removed.

2. Breathing vs respiration: NOT the same!

BreathingRespiration
A physical process: moving air in and out of the lungsA chemical process: breaking down food to release energy
Happens in the lungs (respiratory organs)Happens inside every cell of the body
Takes in oxygen, gives out carbon dioxideUses oxygen, makes carbon dioxide and water
No energy is releasedEnergy is released
Word equation for respiration:
glucose (from food) + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

Inhalation = breathing in (taking in air rich in oxygen). Exhalation = breathing out (giving out air with more carbon dioxide). One inhalation + one exhalation = one breath.

Did you know? When you exercise very hard, your muscles may not get enough oxygen. They then break down glucose without oxygen for a short time, which makes lactic acid, a cause of muscle cramps. A massage or hot water bath helps.

3. The human respiratory system (parts of the lungs)

PartWhat it does
Nostrils and nasal cavityAir enters through the nostrils. Tiny hairs and sticky mucus trap dust and germs. The air is also warmed and moistened. (That is why we should breathe through the nose, not the mouth.)
Windpipe (trachea)A tube that carries air from the throat to the lungs. Rings of cartilage keep it open. A flap (the epiglottis) closes it when we swallow, so food doesn't go "down the wrong way".
Bronchi (singular: bronchus)The windpipe splits into two bronchi, one going into each lung.
BronchiolesSmaller and smaller branches inside the lungs (like the branches of an upside-down tree).
Alveoli (air sacs)Millions of tiny balloon-like sacs at the ends of the bronchioles. Here gas exchange happens: oxygen goes into the blood, carbon dioxide comes out.
LungsTwo spongy, elastic organs in the chest. They are the main respiratory organs.
Ribcage (ribs)A bony cage that protects the lungs and heart and moves when we breathe.
DiaphragmA large, dome-shaped sheet of muscle below the lungs. It forms the floor of the chest and helps us breathe in and out.
Path of air: nostrils → nasal cavity → windpipe → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli (→ oxygen into the blood).

4. How we breathe in and out

Breathing IN (inhalation)Breathing OUT (exhalation)
Ribsmove up and outmove down and in
Diaphragmcontracts, flattens, moves downrelaxes, moves up (dome shape)
Chest spacegets biggergets smaller
Airrushes into the lungsis pushed out of the lungs

Try it: put your hands on your chest and breathe in deeply. You can feel your chest get bigger. Measure round your chest with a tape after breathing in and after breathing out; the chest is bigger after breathing in.

Activity: a model of the lungs

  • Take a plastic bottle with its bottom cut off. Fix a Y-shaped tube through the cap, with a balloon on each branch. Tie a rubber sheet (or a big balloon) over the open bottom.
  • Pull the rubber sheet down: the space inside the bottle gets bigger, air enters and the balloons inflate. This is like breathing in (diaphragm moving down).
  • Push the rubber sheet up: the space gets smaller, air is pushed out and the balloons deflate. This is like breathing out (diaphragm moving up).
  • Bottle = chest/ribcage • Y-tube = windpipe and bronchi • balloons = lungs • rubber sheet = diaphragm.
  • Limitation of the model: the bottle cannot move like the real ribcage does.

Breathing rate

The breathing rate is the number of breaths per minute. Most people at rest breathe about 12–20 times a minute. After running or exercise the rate goes up, because the muscles need more energy, so the body needs more oxygen faster (and must remove more carbon dioxide). It is lower when sleeping. People who are fit often recover their normal rate faster.

5. What do we breathe out? The lime water test

  • Lime water is a clear, colourless solution (of calcium hydroxide).
  • Carbon dioxide turns lime water MILKY (white and cloudy). This is the test for carbon dioxide.
  • Tube A: air from the surroundings pushed in with a syringe/pichkari: lime water stays clear, or changes very slowly (very little CO₂).
  • Tube B: exhaled air blown in through a straw: lime water turns milky quickly.
  • Conclusion: exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than the air we breathe in.
Why milky? carbon dioxide + lime water (calcium hydroxide) → calcium carbonate (a white solid that doesn't dissolve, so the water looks milky) + water.
GasInhaled air (breathed in)Exhaled air (breathed out)
Nitrogenabout 78%about 78% (unchanged)
Oxygenabout 21%about 16% (less: some was used)
Carbon dioxideabout 0.04%about 4% (much more)
Water vapourlessmore (breathe on a mirror and it mists up)

Careful: we do NOT breathe in pure oxygen. We breathe in air, which is only about 21% oxygen. And exhaled air still contains oxygen (that is why mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing works).

6. Breathing in other animals

AnimalBreathes throughHow
FishGillsWater enters the mouth and passes over the gills, which take in the oxygen dissolved in water. Gills have many blood vessels.
Insects (cockroach, grasshopper)Spiracles and tracheaeSmall holes along the sides of the body (spiracles) lead into a network of air tubes (tracheae) that carry air to every part.
EarthwormMoist skinGases pass through its thin, wet, slimy skin. (If its skin dries out, it can't breathe. Rain fills soil with water, so earthworms come up.)
FrogLungs and moist skinLungs on land; through its skin too, especially in water.
Whales, dolphinsLungsThey are mammals, so they come to the surface to breathe air through a blowhole.
BirdsLungs + air sacsAir sacs keep air flowing one way through the lungs, so birds get plenty of oxygen even when flying high, where the air is thin.

So respiration is not the same in all animals: the breathing organs depend on the animal's body size, structure and habitat. But they all take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.

7. Circulation and excretion (the transport and waste system)

  • The heart pumps blood through blood vessels to every part of the body.
  • Blood carries oxygen (from the lungs) and digested food (from the small intestine) to all the cells, and carries carbon dioxide and other wastes away from them.
  • Excretion = removing waste made by the body's cells. The two kidneys filter the blood and make urine, which is stored in the urinary bladder. The lungs excrete carbon dioxide. The skin removes some water and salts as sweat.
  • Excretion ≠ egestion. Egestion is removing undigested food (faeces) through the anus.

8. Keeping our lungs healthy

  • Sneezing pushes out dust or irritating particles trapped in the nose. Cover your mouth and nose when you sneeze, so germs don't spread.
  • Smoking damages the lungs and can cause lung cancer and other diseases. Avoid smoke, including other people's.
  • Air pollution (dust, smoke, vehicle exhaust) harms the lungs, especially for people who work outdoors such as street vendors, farmers and traffic police. Masks help on polluted days.
  • Asthma narrows the airways and makes breathing hard; dust and smoke can trigger it.
  • Regular exercise and breathing outdoors in clean air keep the lungs strong.
  • Box breathing to calm down: breathe in for 4 seconds, hold 4, breathe out 4, hold 4 (repeat).

✅ Quick check: Breathing & Respiration

1. Give two differences between breathing and respiration.

Breathing is physical (moving air in/out of the lungs); respiration is chemical (breaking down food). Respiration releases energy and happens in every cell; breathing releases no energy and uses the lungs.

2. What happens to the ribs and diaphragm when we breathe in?

Ribs move up and out; the diaphragm contracts and moves down (flattens). The chest gets bigger and air rushes in.

3. What colour does lime water turn when you blow into it, and why?

Milky (white and cloudy), because exhaled air contains a lot of carbon dioxide.

4. Where does gas exchange happen in the lungs?

In the alveoli (air sacs).

5. How does an earthworm breathe?

Through its moist skin.

6. Why do we breathe faster after running?

The muscles need more energy, so the body needs more oxygen quickly, and must remove more carbon dioxide.

📽️ Revision slideshow: Investigations

1. Planning a fair test

TermMeaningExample: "Does water temperature affect how fast sugar dissolves?"
Question / aimWhat you want to find outHow does temperature affect dissolving time?
Hypothesis / predictionWhat you think will happen and whyHotter water will dissolve sugar faster, because particles move faster
Independent variableThe one thing you changeWater temperature (20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C)
Dependent variableWhat you measureTime for the sugar to dissolve (s)
Control variablesEverything you keep the sameMass and type of sugar, volume of water, stirring, beaker
Memory trick: "I change the Independent, I measure the Dependent, I Control the rest." A test is fair only if just ONE variable changes.

Reliability: repeat each test (e.g. 3 times) and calculate a mean. Repeats help you spot anomalous results (readings that don't fit the pattern). Accuracy means using the right instruments carefully: read a thermometer at eye level, start and stop the stopwatch at the right moments.

2. Results, graphs and conclusions

  • Record results in a table: independent variable in the first column, with units in the headings (Temperature (°C) | Time (s)).
  • Draw a line graph when both variables are numbers. Put the independent variable on the x-axis (horizontal). Use even scales, plot neatly, and draw a smooth line or curve of best fit.
  • Use a bar chart when the independent variable is a category (types of material, brands).

Writing a strong conclusion

  1. State the pattern: "As the temperature increased, the dissolving time decreased."
  2. Use numbers as evidence: "At 20 °C it took 80 s, but at 60 °C only 32 s."
  3. Explain using science: "At higher temperatures water particles move faster and collide with the sugar more, so it dissolves faster."
  4. Comment on reliability: "The reading at 40 °C (75 s) was anomalous, so it should be repeated."
  5. Suggest an improvement: "Use a water bath to keep the temperature steady; repeat each test three times."
Spot the unfair test: Three groups test dissolving at different temperatures, but one uses crushed sugar and another uses a sugar cube. The test is unfair because particle size also changed, so you can't tell whether temperature or size caused the difference.

3. Analysing diagrams

Follow part → function → interaction → result. Identify the system (a circuit, the digestive system), name each labelled part, say what it does, then explain how the parts work together and what happens if one fails.

1. What do plants need to grow?

Like all living things, plants need food for energy, growth and repair. Unlike animals, green plants make their own food. To grow well they need sunlight, water, air (carbon dioxide) and minerals from the soil.

Pot (Activity 10.1)ConditionsAfter two weeks
ASunlight + waterGrows best — tallest, more green leaves
BSunlight, no waterWilts and may die
CDark + waterGrows less, leaves pale/yellow

So: plants need both sunlight and water to grow.

2. Photosynthesis — leaves are "food factories"

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food (glucose) from carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight, with the help of the green pigment chlorophyll. Oxygen is given out.

carbon dioxide + water —(sunlight, chlorophyll)→ glucose + oxygen
Needed for photosynthesisWhere it comes from
Carbon dioxideAir — enters through stomata
Water (+ minerals)Soil — taken in by roots, carried up by xylem
SunlightThe Sun — trapped by chlorophyll
ChlorophyllGreen pigment in leaves
  • Glucose gives instant energy; extra glucose is changed into starch and stored.
  • That is why a leaf that has been in sunlight turns blue-black with iodine (starch present).
  • Photosynthesis also gives us the oxygen we breathe.

3. Proving what photosynthesis needs

ActivityWhat was doneResultShows that…
10.2 Starch test on a leafBoil leaf in water → put in alcohol (in hot water bath) to remove green colour → add iodineBlue-blackLeaf contains starch (food)
10.3 Variegated leafGreen-and-white leaf; one plant in sunlight, one in dark 36 h; iodine testOnly green parts of the leaf kept in sunlight turn blue-blackChlorophyll and sunlight are needed
10.4 Leaf in a bottle with caustic sodaDestarched plant; half leaf inside a bottle with caustic soda (absorbs CO₂); sunlight; iodine testPart inside bottle: no blue-black; part outside: blue-blackCarbon dioxide is needed
10.5 Water plant under a funnelA in sunlight, B in dark; collect gas; test with a glowing/lit matchstickBubbles only in A; gas makes the flame burn brighterOxygen is given out, and only in light
Why destarch first? Keeping the plant in the dark for 2–3 days uses up its stored starch, so any starch found later must have been made during the experiment. Why alcohol? It removes chlorophyll so the colour change is easy to see. Alcohol catches fire easily — heat it in a water bath, never directly.

4. Stomata — how leaves exchange gases

  • Stomata (singular: stoma) are tiny pores, mostly on the lower surface of leaves.
  • During photosynthesis, carbon dioxide goes in and oxygen comes out through them.
  • During respiration, oxygen goes in and carbon dioxide comes out through them.
  • Water vapour also escapes through stomata.
  • Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells that open and close the pore.

5. Transport in plants — xylem and phloem

XylemPhloem
What it carriesWater and mineralsFood (made in leaves)
From → toFrom the roots up to the stem, leaves and flowersFrom the leaves to all parts (roots, stem, fruits, seeds)
DirectionUpwards onlyUpwards and downwards
ShapeBoth are tube-like tissues — the plant's "pipes"

Activity 10.7 (coloured water): a white-flowered plant (e.g. white sadabahar) stood in water with red ink. After a day the stem, leaf veins and petals turn red, and a cut stem shows red dots — the xylem carried the coloured water up.

Memory trick: PHloem carries Food (phloem is said "flo-em"). Xylem carries water up — like a straw.

6. Do plants respire?

Yes. Every living cell in a plant respires all the time, day and night, to get energy:

glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

Activity 10.8: soaked moong seeds in a closed flask (dark, 24 h); the air from the flask turns lime water milky → the seeds gave out carbon dioxide.

PhotosynthesisRespiration
What happensFood (glucose) is madeFood (glucose) is broken down for energy
Gas taken inCarbon dioxideOxygen
Gas given outOxygenCarbon dioxide
WhenOnly in sunlightAll the time (day and night)
WhereGreen parts (with chlorophyll)Every living cell
EnergyStored (in food)Released

✅ Quick check: Life Processes in Plants

1. Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

carbon dioxide + water —(sunlight, chlorophyll)→ glucose + oxygen

2. Why are leaves called the "food factories" of a plant?

Most photosynthesis happens in leaves — they have chlorophyll, get sunlight, and take in carbon dioxide through stomata.

3. What is the difference between xylem and phloem?

Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots; phloem carries food from the leaves to all parts of the plant.

4. In Activity 10.4, why is caustic soda put in the bottle?

It absorbs carbon dioxide, so the leaf inside gets no CO₂ — showing that CO₂ is needed to make starch.

5. Why do only the green parts of a variegated leaf turn blue-black?

Only the green parts have chlorophyll, which is needed for photosynthesis (making starch).

6. A plant is kept in the dark for 3 days, then a leaf is tested with iodine. What happens and why?

No blue-black colour — without light it couldn't photosynthesise, and it used up its stored starch.

7. Do plants respire at night? How do you know?

Yes — respiration happens all the time. Germinating seeds kept in the dark give out carbon dioxide that turns lime water milky.

8. A white flower stands in red-ink water. Its petals turn red. Which tissue carried the water?

Xylem.

🧪 How to write ANY experiment answer

Every activity below is written in the exam format. Learn the headings in order:

HeadingWhat to write
1. AimOne line starting “To find out…” / “To show that…”.
2. HypothesisYour prediction with a reason: “If…, then…, because…”.
3. MaterialsEverything you need, as a list.
4. DiagramNeat, labelled, pencil and ruler (see the ✏️ Diagrams tab).
5. ProcedureNumbered steps, in order, clear enough for someone else to repeat.
6. ObservationWhat you actually SAW — use a table if you can.
7. ConclusionWhat the result proves. Answer the aim.
8. PrecautionsSafety + things that keep it a fair test.
Fair test words: change only one thing (what you change), observe one thing (what you measure), keep everything else the same. The control is the set-up without the thing you are testing (e.g. rice with no saliva).
