Activity 9.1 · What does saliva do to starch?

🎯 AimTo find out the effect of saliva on starch.
💭 HypothesisIf boiled rice is chewed (mixed with saliva), it will give less blue-black colour with iodine than unchewed rice, because saliva breaks down starch.
🧰 MaterialsTwo test tubes (labelled A and B), test-tube stand, boiled rice, water, iodine solution, dropper, teaspoon.
📋 Procedure
  1. Label the two test tubes A and B.
  2. Put one teaspoon of boiled rice in test tube A.
  3. Chew one teaspoon of boiled rice for 30–60 seconds and put it in test tube B.
  4. Add 3–4 mL of water to each tube. Note the colour of each.
  5. Add 3–4 drops of iodine solution to each tube and shake gently.
  6. Observe the colour and record it in a table.
👀 Observation
Test tubeColour before iodineColour after iodineReason
A (boiled rice)WhitishBlue-blackStarch is present
B (chewed rice)WhitishNo change / very light blue-blackSaliva broke down most of the starch
✅ ConclusionSaliva breaks down starch into simple sugars. That is why chewed rice or chapati starts to taste sweet. Tube A is the control.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Use clean, separate test tubes.
  • Use the same amount of rice and water in both tubes (fair test).
  • Never taste iodine solution.
  • Add iodine with a dropper, a few drops only.
Fair-test words: what we change = saliva (chewed or not) · what we observe = colour with iodine · kept the same = amount of rice, water, iodine · control = tube A.
Try it: chew for longer — the colour becomes even lighter.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw two test tubes side by side with a ruler (rounded bottoms).
  2. Shade tube A dark (blue-black) and tube B pale.
  3. Draw a dropper above each tube.
  4. Label: test tube, iodine solution, boiled rice + water, chewed rice + water.
  5. Write A and B under the tubes and the result under each.

↑ back to the list

Activity 9.2 · Model to show how we breathe

🎯 AimTo make a model that shows the role of the diaphragm in breathing.
💭 HypothesisWhen the rubber sheet (diaphragm) is pulled down, the space inside the bottle increases, so the balloons (lungs) will fill with air.
🧰 MaterialsA wide transparent plastic bottle with lid (base removed), Y-shaped hollow tube, two deflated balloons, rubber bands, a thin rubber sheet, clay.
📋 Procedure
  1. Make a hole in the lid and push the straight end of the Y-tube through it.
  2. Seal the gaps around the tube with clay so it is airtight.
  3. Fix a balloon to each fork of the Y-tube with rubber bands. Put the lid on the bottle.
  4. Tie the rubber sheet tightly over the open base of the bottle.
  5. Pull the rubber sheet down and watch the balloons.
  6. Push the rubber sheet up and watch the balloons.
👀 ObservationRubber sheet pulled down → balloons inflate. Rubber sheet pushed up → balloons deflate.
✅ ConclusionWhen the diaphragm moves down, the chest space gets bigger and air is drawn into the lungs (inhalation). When it moves up, the space gets smaller and air is pushed out (exhalation).
⚠️ Precautions
  • Make the set-up airtight (clay around the tube).
  • Tie the rubber sheet and balloons tightly.
  • Pull and push gently so the balloons don't burst.
Part of modelRepresents
BottleChest cavity (rib cage)
Y-shaped tubeWindpipe, which branches into two
BalloonsLungs
Rubber sheetDiaphragm
Limitation: a real rib cage moves up and out when we breathe in; the bottle can't move.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw the bottle outline (shoulders at the top).
  2. Draw the lid and the Y-tube going through it; split it into two branches.
  3. Draw a round balloon on each branch.
  4. Draw the rubber sheet across the bottom as a curved line.
  5. Add arrows: sheet pulled down (air in) / pushed up (air out).
  6. Label all four parts AND what each represents.

↑ back to the list

Activity 9.3 · What do we breathe out? (lime water test — teacher demonstration)

🎯 AimTo show that the air we breathe out contains more carbon dioxide than the air we breathe in.
💭 HypothesisLime water with exhaled air will turn milky, but lime water with room air will stay clear, because exhaled air has more carbon dioxide.
🧰 MaterialsFreshly prepared lime water, two test tubes (A and B), a syringe or pichkari, a straw.
📋 Procedure
  1. Pour the same amount of fresh lime water into test tubes A and B.
  2. Tube A: pass room air through the lime water using a syringe/pichkari (this is like inhaled air).
  3. Tube B: gently blow air out through a straw into the lime water several times (exhaled air).
  4. Compare the two tubes.
👀 ObservationTube B turns milky (cloudy). Tube A shows no (or very little) change.
✅ ConclusionLime water turns milky with carbon dioxide. Exhaled air contains much more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Use freshly prepared lime water.
  • Blow gently and never suck lime water up the straw.
  • Use equal amounts of lime water in both tubes.
  • This is a teacher demonstration.
GasInhaled airExhaled air
Oxygenabout 21%about 16–17%
Carbon dioxideabout 0.04%about 4–5%
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw two test tubes with liquid about halfway up.
  2. Tube A: syringe tube dipping into the lime water.
  3. Tube B: a straw dipping in, with a face/mouth blowing.
  4. Shade B cloudy (dots); leave A clear.
  5. Label: lime water, syringe, straw, A stays clear, B turns milky.

↑ back to the list

📘 Ch 10 · Life Processes in Plants

Activity 10.1 · What do plants need to grow?

🎯 AimTo find out whether plants need sunlight and water to grow.
💭 HypothesisThe plant with both sunlight and water will grow best; plants without water or light will grow poorly.
🧰 MaterialsThree equal pots with garden soil, three similar saplings (chilli or tomato), water.
📋 Procedure
  1. Label the pots A, B and C; plant one sapling in each and count the leaves.
  2. A: keep in sunlight and water daily.
  3. B: keep in sunlight but do not water.
  4. C: keep in the dark and water daily.
  5. Observe for two weeks; record height, number of leaves and leaf colour.
👀 ObservationA grows best. C grows less and its leaves turn pale. B wilts and may die.
✅ ConclusionPlants need both sunlight and water to grow.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Use similar saplings and equal pots (fair test).
  • Give A and C the same amount of water.

↑ back to the list

Activity 10.2 · Testing a leaf for starch (demonstration)

🎯 AimTo test a green leaf for the presence of starch.
💭 HypothesisA leaf that has been in sunlight will contain starch and turn blue-black with iodine.
🧰 MaterialsA leaf, boiling water, alcohol, test tube, beaker, spirit lamp, wire gauze, dilute iodine solution, dropper, plate.
📋 Procedure
  1. Boil the leaf in water for about 5 minutes to soften it.
  2. Put the leaf in a test tube of alcohol and stand the test tube in a beaker of boiling water until the leaf loses its green colour.
  3. Wash the leaf, spread it on a plate and add a few drops of iodine solution.
👀 ObservationThe leaf turns blue-black.
✅ ConclusionThe leaf contains starch. Removing the green colour makes the change easy to see.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Alcohol catches fire easily — never heat it directly over a flame; use a water bath.
  • Teacher demonstration.

↑ back to the list

Activity 10.3 · Are chlorophyll and sunlight needed?

🎯 AimTo show that chlorophyll and sunlight are needed to make starch.
💭 HypothesisOnly the green parts of a leaf kept in sunlight will turn blue-black with iodine.
🧰 MaterialsTwo similar potted plants with variegated (green and white) leaves, tracing paper, iodine test materials.
📋 Procedure
  1. Keep one plant in sunlight and the other in the dark for 36 hours.
  2. Trace the green and white patches of a leaf from each plant on tracing paper.
  3. Do the iodine test on both leaves and compare with your tracings.
👀 ObservationSunlight leaf: green patches turn blue-black, white patches don't. Dark leaf: no blue-black anywhere.
✅ ConclusionBoth chlorophyll and sunlight are needed for photosynthesis.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Use similar leaves.
  • Follow the iodine-test safety steps.

↑ back to the list

Activity 10.4 · Is carbon dioxide needed? (demonstration)

🎯 AimTo show that carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis.
💭 HypothesisThe part of the leaf that gets no carbon dioxide will not make starch.
🧰 MaterialsPotted green plant, wide-mouthed bottle, caustic soda (absorbs CO₂), split cork, iodine test materials.
📋 Procedure
  1. Keep the plant in the dark for 2–3 days (destarch it).
  2. Put caustic soda in the bottle.
  3. Push half of one leaf into the bottle through a split cork; the other half stays outside.
  4. Keep the set-up in sunlight for a few hours.
  5. Do the iodine test on the whole leaf.
👀 ObservationThe half outside turns blue-black; the half inside does not.
✅ ConclusionCarbon dioxide is needed to make starch.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Caustic soda burns skin — only the teacher handles it.
  • Seal the cork well so air can't get in.

↑ back to the list

Activity 10.5 · Is oxygen given out? (water plant)

🎯 AimTo show that oxygen is released during photosynthesis.
💭 HypothesisA water plant in sunlight will give out bubbles of oxygen; in the dark it will not.
🧰 MaterialsWater plant (e.g. hydrilla), two beakers, two funnels, two test tubes, water.
📋 Procedure
  1. Place the water plant under an upside-down funnel in a beaker of water; cover the funnel with a test tube full of water.
  2. Keep set-up A in sunlight and set-up B in the dark.
  3. Watch for bubbles; collect the gas.
  4. Bring a lit matchstick near the gas.
👀 ObservationBubbles appear only in A. The gas makes the matchstick burn more brightly.
✅ ConclusionPlants give out oxygen during photosynthesis, which happens only in light.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Keep the test tube full of water at the start.
  • Teacher handles the matchstick.

↑ back to the list

Activity 10.6 · Looking at stomata (demonstration)

🎯 AimTo observe stomata on a leaf.
💭 HypothesisTiny pores will be seen on the lower surface of the leaf.
🧰 MaterialsLeaf of rhoeo/money plant/hibiscus, forceps, glass slide, water, a drop of ink, coverslip, microscope.
📋 Procedure
  1. Peel a thin layer from the lower surface of the leaf.
  2. Put it on a slide in a drop of water; add a drop of ink.
  3. Cover with a coverslip and look under the microscope.
👀 ObservationMany tiny pores are seen.
✅ ConclusionThese pores are stomata; they let gases in and out of the leaf.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Use a thin peel.
  • Lower the coverslip gently to avoid air bubbles.

↑ back to the list

Activity 10.7 · How does water travel up a plant?

🎯 AimTo show that water and minerals travel up the stem through the xylem.
💭 HypothesisColoured water will travel up the stem into the leaves and flowers.
🧰 MaterialsTwo tumblers, water, red ink, two tender white-flowered plants (white sadabahar or balsam), magnifying glass.
📋 Procedure
  1. Fill both tumblers one-third with water; add red ink to tumbler B.
  2. Cut the stems at a slant under water and stand one plant in each tumbler.
  3. After one day, observe; then cut the stem and look at the cut end with a magnifying glass.
👀 ObservationThe plant in red water shows red in its stem, leaf veins and flowers; the cut stem shows red spots.
✅ ConclusionWater and minerals move up through the xylem.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Cut stems under water so air doesn't block them.
  • Tumbler A is the control.

↑ back to the list

Activity 10.8 · Do plants respire? (germinating seeds)

🎯 AimTo show that germinating seeds give out carbon dioxide during respiration.
💭 HypothesisAir from the flask of germinating seeds will turn lime water milky.
🧰 MaterialsSoaked moong seeds, conical flask, moist cotton, cork with two holes, glass tubes, rubber pipe, two test tubes, lime water.
📋 Procedure
  1. Soak the seeds overnight and place them on moist cotton in the flask.
  2. Close the flask with the cork and keep it in the dark for 24 hours.
  3. Connect the flask to test tube A containing lime water; tube B has lime water only (control).
  4. Observe.
👀 ObservationLime water in tube A turns milky; tube B stays clear.
✅ ConclusionGerminating seeds respire and give out carbon dioxide.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Keep it airtight.
  • Kept in the dark so photosynthesis can't use up the CO₂.

↑ back to the list

📘 Ch 11 · Light: Shadows and Reflections

Activity 11.1 · Does light travel in a straight line?

🎯 AimTo show that light travels in a straight line.
💭 HypothesisThe torch light will reach the screen only when all three holes are in a straight line.
🧰 MaterialsThree matchboxes (inner trays), a torch, a cardboard screen, a pin to make the holes.
📋 Procedure
  1. Make a small hole at the same spot in the inner tray of each matchbox.
  2. Stand the trays in a line so the holes are at the same height and in a straight line.
  3. Place the torch on one side at the height of the holes; place the screen on the other side.
  4. Switch on the torch (in a dim room) and look for a bright spot on the screen.
  5. Move one matchbox slightly sideways or up/down and look again.
👀 ObservationA bright spot is seen only when all three holes are in a straight line. When one box is moved, the spot disappears.
✅ ConclusionLight travels in a straight line.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Make the holes the same size and at the same height.
  • Do it in a dim room so the spot is easy to see.
  • Don't shine the torch into anyone's eyes.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw the torch on the left and the screen on the right.
  2. Draw three tall rectangles (trays) between them, evenly spaced.
  3. Mark a hole at the same height in each.
  4. Draw ONE straight ruler line (light) through all holes to the screen.
  5. Mark the bright spot and label everything.

↑ back to the list

Activity 11.2 · Looking at a candle flame through a pipe

🎯 AimTo show that light travels in a straight line.
💭 HypothesisThe flame will be seen through a straight pipe but not through a bent pipe.
🧰 MaterialsA flexible hollow pipe, a lit candle (with an adult).
📋 Procedure
  1. Light a candle (with adult supervision).
  2. Look at the flame through the pipe kept straight.
  3. Now bend the pipe and look again.
👀 ObservationThe flame is visible through the straight pipe but not through the bent pipe.
✅ ConclusionLight travels in a straight line; it cannot go round the bend.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Adult supervision with the flame.
  • Keep hair, paper and the pipe away from the flame.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw a candle on the left and an eye on the right.
  2. (a) Draw a straight pipe between them with a dashed straight light line.
  3. (b) Draw a bent pipe; the dashed light line stops at the bend.
  4. Mark ✔ for seen and ✘ for not seen.

↑ back to the list

Activity 11.3 · Light through different materials

🎯 AimTo classify materials as transparent, translucent or opaque.
💭 HypothesisLight will pass through glass fully, through tracing paper partly, and not at all through cardboard.
🧰 MaterialsA torch, a screen or wall, a dark room, and objects: glass, tracing paper, paper, cardboard, thick cloth.
📋 Procedure
  1. Predict for each material: will light pass through fully, partly or not at all? Write it in a table.
  2. In a dark room, hold each object between the torch and the screen.
  3. Observe how much light reaches the screen and record it next to your prediction.
👀 Observation
MaterialLight passesType
Clear glassAlmost completelyTransparent
Tracing paper, butter paper, frosted glassPartlyTranslucent
Cardboard, thick cloth, woodNot at allOpaque
✅ ConclusionTransparent materials let light pass almost completely, translucent materials partly, opaque materials not at all.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Do it in a dark room.
  • Keep the torch at the same distance for every material (fair test).
  • If a teacher uses a laser, never point it at eyes.

↑ back to the list

Activity 11.4 · What affects a shadow?

🎯 AimTo find out what is needed to form a shadow and what changes its size and shape.
💭 HypothesisA shadow will form only when there is a light source, an opaque object and a screen; moving the object will change the shadow's size.
🧰 MaterialsA torch, opaque objects of different shapes and sizes, a screen.
📋 Procedure
  1. Place an opaque object between the torch and the screen; see its shadow.
  2. Do each change below, one at a time, and record what happens to the shadow.
👀 Observation
What you doWhat happens
Remove the screenNo shadow can be seen
Remove the objectNo shadow
Switch off the torchNo shadow
Use an object of another colourShadow is still dark — colour does not change
Move the object closer to the screenShadow gets smaller and sharper
Move the object closer to the torchShadow gets bigger
Tilt / turn the objectShadow's shape changes
✅ ConclusionA shadow needs three things: a light source, an opaque object and a screen. Its size, shape and sharpness depend on the object's position. The colour of the object does not change the colour of the shadow.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Change only ONE thing at a time.
  • Keep the torch fixed in one place.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw the torch on the left and the screen on the right.
  2. Draw the object in between.
  3. Draw two straight ruler lines from the torch past the TOP and BOTTOM edges of the object to the screen.
  4. Shade the part of the screen between those lines dark = shadow.
  5. Label: light source, opaque object, screen, shadow.

↑ back to the list

Activity 11.5 · Changing the direction of sunlight

🎯 AimTo show that a shiny surface changes the direction of light.
💭 HypothesisA mirror placed in sunlight will send a patch of light onto a wall where sunlight does not fall.
🧰 MaterialsA plane mirror or a shiny flat steel plate, sunlight.
📋 Procedure
  1. Hold the mirror in sunlight.
  2. Turn it slowly until a bright patch of light falls on a shaded wall.
👀 ObservationA bright patch appears on the shaded wall; it moves when the mirror is tilted.
✅ ConclusionA mirror (shiny surface) changes the direction of light falling on it. This is called reflection.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Never reflect sunlight into anyone's eyes.
  • Hold the mirror carefully by its edges.

↑ back to the list

Activity 11.6 · Reflection of a thin beam by a plane mirror

🎯 AimTo observe the reflection of light by a plane mirror.
💭 HypothesisThe thin beam of light will change direction when it hits the mirror.
🧰 MaterialsPlane mirror with stand, torch, comb, white paper, black paper strip.
📋 Procedure
  1. Cover all the gaps of the comb with black paper except one (to make a thin slit).
  2. Stand the comb on a sheet of white paper.
  3. Shine the torch through the slit to get a thin beam on the paper.
  4. Place the mirror in the path of the beam.
  5. Tilt the mirror in different ways and watch the beam.
👀 ObservationThe beam changes direction at the mirror. Tilting the mirror changes the direction of the reflected beam.
✅ ConclusionLight is reflected by a plane mirror; the incoming beam is the incident beam and the outgoing one is the reflected beam.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Do it in a dim room so the beam shows clearly.
  • Keep the mirror standing straight (upright).
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw a long rectangle for the mirror; add short slanted lines on the BACK side.
  2. Draw the incident beam with a ruler and an arrow towards the mirror.
  3. Draw the reflected beam from the same point, arrow going away.
  4. Label: plane mirror, incident beam, reflected beam.

↑ back to the list

Activity 11.7 · The image of a pen in a plane mirror

🎯 AimTo find the features of an image formed by a plane mirror.
💭 HypothesisThe image will be the same size as the pen and upright, and it can't be caught on a screen.
🧰 MaterialsA plane mirror, a pen, a screen (card).
📋 Procedure
  1. Stand the pen in front of the mirror and look at its image.
  2. Move the pen to different positions; compare the size of the image with the pen. Is it upright?
  3. Try to catch the image on a screen — first behind the mirror, then in front of it.
👀 ObservationThe image is the same size as the pen and upright, at every position. It cannot be obtained on the screen.
✅ ConclusionA plane mirror forms an image that is the same size, erect (upright), and cannot be obtained on a screen.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Keep the mirror upright.
  • Use a clean mirror.

↑ back to the list

Activity 11.8 · How far away is the image? (lateral inversion)

🎯 AimTo find the distance of the image and to observe lateral inversion.
💭 HypothesisThe image will be as far behind the mirror as I am in front of it, and my left and right will look swapped.
🧰 MaterialsA plane mirror (large enough to see yourself).
📋 Procedure
  1. Stand at different distances from the mirror and notice how far away your image seems.
  2. Raise your left arm and touch your right ear; see which hand your image uses.
👀 ObservationThe image seems as far behind the mirror as you stand in front of it. Your image seems to use its right hand to touch its left ear.
✅ ConclusionThe image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Left and right appear swapped: lateral inversion.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Stand straight in front of the mirror.
  • Handle a large mirror with care.
Real-life use: AMBULANCE is written backwards on the front of ambulances so drivers ahead read it correctly in their rear-view mirror.

↑ back to the list

Activity 11.9 · Candle flame through a pinhole

🎯 AimTo observe the image of a candle flame formed through a pinhole.
💭 HypothesisLight from the flame will pass through the tiny hole and form an upside-down image on the screen.
🧰 MaterialsCardboard with a small hole, a screen, a lit candle (with an adult).
📋 Procedure
  1. In a dim room, light the candle (with adult supervision).
  2. Place the cardboard between the candle and the screen, a short distance apart.
  3. Adjust until an image of the flame appears on the screen.
👀 ObservationAn image of the flame appears on the screen, upside down.
✅ ConclusionLight travels in straight lines through the pinhole, so the image is inverted.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Adult supervision with the flame.
  • Keep the hole small.
  • Work in a dim room.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw the candle (left), cardboard with a hole (middle), screen (right).
  2. Ray 1: straight line from the flame TIP through the hole to the screen (it lands LOW).
  3. Ray 2: straight line from the candle BASE through the hole (it lands HIGH). The rays cross at the hole.
  4. Draw the small upside-down candle on the screen between the two rays.
  5. Label: candle, pinhole, screen, inverted image.

↑ back to the list

Activity 11.10 · Make a sliding pinhole camera

🎯 AimTo make a pinhole camera and observe the image of a distant object.
💭 HypothesisThe image of the object on the tracing paper will be upside down.
🧰 MaterialsTwo cardboard boxes that slide one inside the other, tracing paper, a dark cloth, a pin.
📋 Procedure
  1. Make a pinhole in the middle of one face of the larger box.
  2. Cut a window in the smaller box and cover it with tracing paper (this is the screen).
  3. Slide the smaller box into the larger one, tracing-paper side inside.
  4. Point the pinhole at a distant object in bright sunlight; cover your head and the camera's open end with the dark cloth.
  5. Slide the smaller box in or out until a clear image appears on the tracing paper.
👀 ObservationA small image of the object appears on the tracing paper. It is upside down and has the same colours as the object.
✅ ConclusionA pinhole camera forms an inverted image because light travels in straight lines.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Never look at the Sun through it.
  • Keep the pinhole small for a sharp image.
  • Use the dark cloth to block extra light.

↑ back to the list

Activity Make it · Periscope and kaleidoscope

🎯 AimTo make a periscope to see objects that are not directly in view.
💭 HypothesisTwo mirrors at 45° will send light down the tube to my eye, so I can see over a wall.
🧰 MaterialsA long box/tube bent into a Z shape (or card), two plane mirrors, tape.
📋 Procedure
  1. Cut openings at the top front and bottom back of a Z-shaped tube.
  2. Fix mirror 1 at the top at 45°, facing down the tube.
  3. Fix mirror 2 at the bottom at 45°, facing mirror 1 (the two mirrors are parallel).
  4. Look into the bottom opening.
👀 ObservationYou can see objects above or round an obstacle.
✅ ConclusionLight is reflected twice (by two mirrors) to reach the eye. Periscopes are used in submarines, tanks and by soldiers in bunkers.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Fix the mirrors firmly at exactly 45°.
  • Handle mirrors by the edges.
Kaleidoscope: three mirror strips joined in a triangle inside a tube, with coloured glass pieces at one end. Multiple reflections make beautiful, changing patterns.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw the Z-shaped tube with a ruler.
  2. Draw two short thick lines at 45° in the two corners — make them parallel.
  3. Draw the light ray: straight in → down the tube → out to the eye, with arrows.
  4. Label: mirror 1, mirror 2, object, eye.

↑ back to the list

📘 Ch 3 · Electricity: Circuits and their Components

Activity 3.1 · Exploring a torch

🎯 AimTo find out the parts of a torch and how its switch works.
💭 HypothesisThe lamp will glow in one position of the switch and not in the other.
🧰 MaterialsA torch.
📋 Procedure
  1. Find the lamp and the switch.
  2. Slide the switch one way and observe the lamp; slide it back and observe again.
  3. Open the torch and look inside.
👀 ObservationThe lamp glows in one switch position only. Inside there are two or more electric cells.
✅ ConclusionA torch has cells (source of electricity), a switch and a lamp. The switch turns the lamp on and off.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Close the torch properly after looking inside.

↑ back to the list

Activity 3.2 · Looking at an electric cell

🎯 AimTo identify the terminals of an electric cell.
💭 HypothesisThe cell will have a positive (+) and a negative (−) end.
🧰 MaterialsAn electric cell.
📋 Procedure
  1. Turn the cell over and look at both ends.
  2. Look for the + and − signs.
👀 ObservationOne end has a small metal cap (+) and the other a flat metal disc (−).
✅ ConclusionA cell has two terminals: the metal cap is the positive terminal; the flat disc is the negative terminal. A cell is a portable source of electrical energy.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Never open a cell.
  • Never use mains electricity for experiments.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw a long rectangle (cell body).
  2. Add a small cap on one end: write +; flat end: write −.
  3. Label: positive terminal (metal cap), negative terminal (flat metal disc).
  4. Next to it draw the symbol: LONG line (+), short thick line (−).

↑ back to the list

Activity 3.3 · Arranging cells in a torch

🎯 AimTo find out how cells must be placed to make a battery.
💭 HypothesisThe lamp will glow only when the cells are placed in the right order.
🧰 MaterialsA torch that uses two cells.
📋 Procedure
  1. Take out the cells.
  2. Put them back in different orders, and with one cell reversed.
  3. Each time, switch on and check the lamp.
👀 ObservationThe lamp glows only when the positive terminal of one cell touches the negative terminal of the next.
✅ ConclusionTwo or more cells joined + to − make a battery. More cells supply more energy and/or for a longer time.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Don't force the cells in.
  • Use cells of the same type.

↑ back to the list

Activity 3.4 · Inside an incandescent lamp

🎯 AimTo observe the parts of an incandescent (filament) lamp.
💭 HypothesisA thin wire inside the lamp will glow when the torch is on.
🧰 MaterialsA torch with an incandescent lamp (check with your teacher).
📋 Procedure
  1. Look closely at the lamp.
  2. Switch on the torch and see which part glows.
  3. With your teacher's help, take out the lamp and look at how the filament is held.
👀 ObservationA thin wire (the filament) glows. It is held by two thicker wires: one joined to the metal case, the other to the metal tip. The two terminals don't touch.
✅ ConclusionWhen current passes, the filament gets very hot and glows, giving light.
⚠️ Precautions
  • The lamp gets hot — let it cool before touching.
  • Handle the glass bulb carefully.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw a pear-shaped glass bulb on top of a short metal case.
  2. Draw two thick wires going up inside.
  3. Join their tops with a zigzag = filament.
  4. Draw a small bead (insulator) holding the wires and a round tip under the case.
  5. Label: glass bulb, filament, thick wires, insulator, metal case (terminal), metal tip (terminal).

↑ back to the list

Activity 3.5 · Looking at an LED

🎯 AimTo observe the structure of an LED.
💭 HypothesisAn LED will have no filament and its two wires will be different.
🧰 MaterialsAn LED of any colour.
📋 Procedure
  1. Look inside the LED for a filament.
  2. Compare the lengths of its two wires (legs).
👀 ObservationAn LED has no filament. One wire is longer than the other.
✅ ConclusionThe longer wire is the positive terminal; the shorter wire is the negative terminal.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Don't bend the legs too much — they can break.

↑ back to the list

Activity 3.6 · Lighting a lamp with a cell

🎯 AimTo find out how to connect a cell and a lamp so that the lamp glows.
💭 HypothesisThe lamp will glow only when there is a complete path from one terminal of the cell, through the lamp, to the other terminal.
🧰 MaterialsAn electric cell, an incandescent lamp, a cell holder, a lamp holder, four connecting wires (or electrical tape).
📋 Procedure
  1. Remove about 1 cm of plastic from both ends of each wire.
  2. Attach two wires to the cell holder; put the cell in with its negative end towards the spring.
  3. Attach two wires to the lamp holder screws and fix the lamp.
  4. Predict whether the lamp will glow for each arrangement in the table.
  5. Connect each arrangement and observe.
👀 ObservationThe lamp glows only in arrangements where both lamp terminals are joined to both cell terminals.
✅ ConclusionA lamp glows only in a complete (closed) path — an electric circuit. Current flows from the + terminal, through the lamp, to the − terminal.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Use only cells/batteries — never the mains supply.
  • Make sure stripped ends touch firmly.
  • Don't join the two cell terminals directly with a wire.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Use a RULER — circuit wires are straight lines with square corners.
  2. Draw the cell symbol on top (long line +).
  3. Draw the lamp symbol (circle with ×) on the opposite side.
  4. Join them into a closed rectangle.
  5. Optional: arrow for current from + round to −.

↑ back to the list

Activity 3.7 · Lighting an LED

🎯 AimTo find out how to connect an LED so that it glows.
💭 HypothesisThe LED will glow only when its longer wire is joined to the positive terminal of the battery.
🧰 MaterialsTwo cells, a holder for two cells, an LED, two wires.
📋 Procedure
  1. Strip the wire ends and attach them to the cell holder; insert both cells with negative ends towards the springs.
  2. Find the positive terminal of the battery.
  3. Join the battery's + to the LED's longer wire and − to the shorter wire. Observe.
  4. Swap the LED's wires and observe again.
👀 ObservationThe LED glows in the first arrangement but not when the wires are swapped.
✅ ConclusionCurrent passes through an LED in one direction only, so it must be connected the right way round.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Use only cells.
  • Check the legs before connecting.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw the LED symbol: a triangle pointing towards a bar, with two small arrows going outwards (light).
  2. Make the triangle point from + towards − in your circuit.

↑ back to the list

Activity 3.8 & 3.9 · Make and test a simple switch

🎯 AimTo make a simple switch and test how it works in a circuit.
💭 HypothesisThe lamp will glow only when the safety pin touches both drawing pins.
🧰 MaterialsTwo drawing pins, a safety pin (or paper clip), a piece of cardboard, wires, a cell, a lamp.
📋 Procedure
  1. Push one drawing pin through the ring of the safety pin and fix it on the cardboard so the pin can turn freely.
  2. Fix the second drawing pin so the free end of the safety pin can touch it.
  3. Join a wire to each drawing pin. Your switch is ready.
  4. 3.9: connect the cell, lamp and switch in a circuit. Observe.
  5. Turn the safety pin so it touches the second drawing pin. Observe.
👀 ObservationThe lamp glows only when the safety pin touches both drawing pins.
✅ ConclusionSwitch ON = closed circuit, current flows. Switch OFF = gap = open circuit, no current. A switch can be placed anywhere in the circuit.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Use only cells.
  • Press the drawing pins in carefully (sharp).
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Switch OFF symbol: dot – line slanted up – gap – dot.
  2. Switch ON symbol: dot – straight line – dot.
  3. Draw the full circuit: cell + lamp + switch in one closed loop.

↑ back to the list

Activity 3.10 · Drawing circuit diagrams

🎯 AimTo draw circuits using standard symbols.
💭 HypothesisAny circuit can be shown simply using symbols.
🧰 MaterialsPencil, ruler, Table 3.2 symbols.
📋 Procedure
  1. Draw a circuit diagram for the circuit with a lamp and a switch.
  2. Draw a circuit diagram for the LED circuit.
  3. Compare your drawings with the book's diagrams.
👀 ObservationEach part is replaced by its symbol and joined by straight lines.
✅ ConclusionA circuit diagram shows a circuit using symbols; it is quick to draw and anyone can read it.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Use a ruler; keep corners square.
  • Show + and − correctly for cells and LEDs.

↑ back to the list

Activity 3.11 · Conductor or insulator? (conduction tester)

🎯 AimTo find out which materials let electric current pass through them.
💭 HypothesisThe lamp will glow with metal objects (conductors) and not with plastic, rubber, wood etc. (insulators).
🧰 MaterialsA cell, a lamp, wires; test objects: metal spoon, coin, key, pins, needle, aluminium foil, pencil lead, cork, rubber, glass, plastic scale, wooden block, candle, cardboard, paper.
📋 Procedure
  1. Make a tester: a cell and lamp joined with wires, leaving two wire ends free.
  2. Touch the free ends together — the lamp should glow (tester works).
  3. Touch the free ends to the two ends of each object.
  4. Record: material, does the lamp glow?, conductor or insulator.
👀 Observation
Lamp glows (conductors)Lamp does not glow (insulators)
Metal spoon, coin, key, safety pin, needle, aluminium foil, pencil lead (graphite)Cork, rubber, glass, plastic scale, wood, candle (wax), cardboard, paper
✅ ConclusionConductors (all metals, and pencil lead) allow current to pass easily; insulators (plastic, rubber, wood, glass, ceramics) do not. Copper is used for wires; plastic covers them.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Don't let the two free wire ends touch each other while testing.
  • Use only cells, never mains electricity.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw the cell, lamp and two wires with free ends.
  2. Draw the object between the free ends.
  3. Label: cell, lamp, free ends, object being tested.

↑ back to the list

📘 Ch 2 · Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic and Neutral

Activity 2.1 · Testing substances with litmus paper

🎯 AimTo find out whether substances are acidic, basic or neutral using litmus paper.
💭 HypothesisSour substances like lemon juice will turn blue litmus red; soapy substances will turn red litmus blue.
🧰 MaterialsLemon juice, soap solution, amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar, baking soda solution, lime water, tap water, washing powder solution, sugar solution, salt solution; blue and red litmus paper; a clean white tile; a dropper.
📋 Procedure
  1. Cut blue litmus paper into small pieces and spread them on the tile.
  2. Put one drop of each sample on a separate piece. Record the colour.
  3. Repeat with red litmus paper.
  4. Sort the samples into Groups A, B and C.
👀 Observation
GroupLitmus resultSamplesNature
ABlue → redLemon juice, amla juice, tamarind water, vinegarAcidic
BRed → blueSoap solution, baking soda, lime water, washing powderBasic
CNo changeTap water, sugar solution, salt solutionNeutral
✅ ConclusionAcids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue; neutral substances change neither.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Never taste the samples.
  • Clean the dropper between samples.
  • Use a fresh piece of litmus for each drop.
✏️ How to draw this diagram:
  1. Draw a rectangle (tile) with two rows of small squares: blue litmus top, red litmus bottom.
  2. Draw a drop on each square; colour the drops by result.
  3. Label: white tile, blue litmus, red litmus, sample names.

↑ back to the list

Activity 2.2 · Taste and touch of acids and bases (relate & explore)

🎯 AimTo relate the properties of acids and bases to everyday experience.
💭 HypothesisGroup A substances will taste sour and baking soda solution will feel slippery.
🧰 MaterialsGroup A foods (from memory), baking soda solution.
📋 Procedure
  1. Recall the taste of Group A foods (lemon, amla, tamarind, vinegar) — don't taste anything now.
  2. Find the acids in lemon, curd, tamarind and vinegar.
  3. Rub a little baking soda solution between your fingers.
👀 ObservationGroup A foods taste sour. Baking soda solution feels soapy / slippery.
✅ ConclusionSour substances are usually acidic; bases feel soapy. But bitter taste does NOT always mean a base (bitter gourd isn't).
⚠️ Precautions
  • Never taste unknown substances.
  • Wash hands afterwards.
FoodAcid in it
Lemon, orange, amlaCitric acid (amla also has ascorbic acid)
CurdLactic acid
TamarindTartaric acid
VinegarAcetic acid

↑ back to the list

Activity 2.3 & 2.4 · Make red rose extract and test with it

🎯 AimTo prepare a natural indicator from red rose petals and use it to test substances.
💭 HypothesisRed rose extract will show one colour in acids and a different colour in bases.
🧰 MaterialsFallen red rose petals, water, mortar and pestle, glass tumbler, hot water, lid, filter; two test tubes A and B, droppers, samples from Activity 2.1.
📋 Procedure
  1. 2.3: Collect fallen petals (don't pluck flowers) and wash a fistful.
  2. Crush them with a mortar and pestle and put them in a tumbler.
  3. Pour in hot water to cover them, cover with a lid and wait 5–10 minutes.
  4. Filter it: the coloured liquid is the red rose extract.
  5. 2.4: Put 10–20 drops of extract in tubes A and B.
  6. Add 20–30 drops of lemon juice to A and 20–30 drops of soap solution to B. Note the colours.
  7. Repeat with the other samples.
👀 ObservationWith lemon juice (acid) the extract turns red; with soap solution (base) it turns green. Neutral samples: no change.
✅ ConclusionRed rose extract is a natural indicator: red in acids, green in bases.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Hot water only with an adult.
  • Use fallen petals.
  • Same number of drops in each tube (fair test).

↑ back to the list

Activity 2.5 · Turmeric paper as an indicator

🎯 AimTo prepare turmeric paper and use it to test substances.
💭 HypothesisTurmeric paper will change colour with bases.
🧰 MaterialsTurmeric powder (or fresh turmeric), water, petri dish, filter paper, scissors, droppers, samples.
📋 Procedure
  1. Make a paste of turmeric and water in a petri dish.
  2. Dip filter paper in the paste until it turns yellow; let it dry.
  3. Cut it into thin strips.
  4. Put one drop of each sample on a separate strip and record.
👀 ObservationBasic samples turn turmeric paper red. Acidic and neutral samples leave it yellow.
✅ ConclusionTurmeric detects bases only; it can't tell an acid from a neutral substance.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Prepare under adult supervision.
  • Turmeric stains — protect clothes.

↑ back to the list

Activity 2.6 · Olfactory (smell) indicators

🎯 AimTo find out whether the smell of onion changes with acids and bases.
💭 HypothesisThe onion smell on a cloth strip will change with an acid or a base.
🧰 MaterialsFinely chopped onion, a tightly closed container, clean cotton cloth or filter paper strips, tamarind water, baking soda solution.
📋 Procedure
  1. Keep the onion and strips together in a closed container overnight.
  2. Smell two strips.
  3. Put tamarind water on one strip and baking soda solution on the other.
  4. Smell them again and compare.
👀 ObservationThe smell of one strip changes after adding the test liquid (record what you notice for each).
✅ ConclusionSome substances change their smell in acids or bases — these are olfactory indicators (useful for people who can't see colours).
⚠️ Precautions
  • Smell gently by wafting, not by sniffing hard.
  • Don't touch your eyes after handling onion.

↑ back to the list

Activity 2.7 · Neutralisation

🎯 AimTo show that a base neutralises an acid.
💭 HypothesisAdding lime water (base) slowly to an acid will make the litmus colour change from red back to blue.
🧰 MaterialsLemon juice, water, a test tube, a dropper, blue litmus solution, lime water.
📋 Procedure
  1. Add one drop of lemon juice to about 20 drops of water in a test tube.
  2. Add a drop of blue litmus solution — it turns red (acidic).
  3. Add lime water drop by drop, swirling after each drop.
  4. Watch for the colour change.
  5. Add one more drop of lemon juice — predict what happens.
👀 ObservationAt one stage the colour changes from red to blue. One more drop of lemon juice turns it red again.
✅ ConclusionThe base (lime water) neutralises the acid. Acid + Base → Salt + Water + Heat.
⚠️ Precautions
  • Add lime water one drop at a time.
  • Swirl gently.
  • Don't taste anything.
Neutralisation in daily life: red-ant bite (formic acid) → rub moist baking soda · acidic soil (too much fertiliser) → add lime · basic soil → add manure/compost · factory acidic waste → neutralised with bases before release.

✏️ Golden rules for science diagrams

  • Use a sharp pencil — never pen or colour for the outline.
  • Draw big: about half a page. Small diagrams lose marks.
  • Use a ruler for label lines, light rays and circuit wires.
  • Label lines are straight, horizontal where possible, and must not cross each other.
  • Write labels on the side, one under another, in neat print. The line must touch the exact part.
  • Give every diagram a title underneath (e.g. “Fig: Human digestive system”).
  • Light rays and current get arrows. Circuits have square corners and no gaps.
  • Only shade where it shows something (iodine colour, milky lime water, shadow).

🫁 Life Processes in Animals

1. Human digestive system

🏷️ Labels to include:
Mouth Oesophagus (food pipe) Liver Gall bladder Stomach Pancreas Small intestine Large intestine Rectum Anus

✏️ Steps to draw it:
  1. Draw the head outline and mouth at the top.
  2. Draw the food pipe as two parallel lines going down the middle.
  3. Draw a J-shaped bag (stomach) on the person's LEFT side (your right).
  4. Draw the large liver on the other side, just above the stomach, with the small gall bladder under it.
  5. Draw the pancreas as a leaf shape just under the stomach.
  6. Draw the large intestine as an upside-down U frame (up, across, down).
  7. Fill the space inside with a coiled tube = small intestine.
  8. Draw the rectum going down and end with the anus.
  9. Add label lines with a ruler on both sides; write the title.

❌ Common mistakes:

  • Drawing the stomach on the wrong side.
  • Making the small intestine shorter or wider than the large intestine (small = long + narrow + coiled).
  • Forgetting the liver/pancreas or joining food to pass through them (food never goes through them).

2. Food pipe and stomach

🏷️ Labels to include:
Site of contraction Food Site of relaxation Stomach wall Digestive juice, acid and mucus

✏️ Steps to draw it:
  1. Draw the food pipe as two wavy parallel lines.
  2. Draw a lump of food inside, with the pipe squeezed narrow just ABOVE it.
  3. Mark contraction above the food and relaxation below; add an arrow pointing down.
  4. Draw the stomach as a J-shaped bag with a thick wall; add small arrows on the inner wall for juices.

❌ Common mistakes:

  • Putting the contraction below the food (it pushes from above).
  • Saying digestion happens in the food pipe — it doesn't.

3. Inner lining of the small intestine (villi)

🏷️ Labels to include:
Villi (finger-like projections) Blood vessels Thin wall

✏️ Steps to draw it:
  1. Draw a horizontal base line.
  2. Draw a row of tall, thin finger shapes standing on it.
  3. Draw a branching red line (blood vessel) inside each.
  4. Label one villus clearly; write: increases surface area for absorption.

❌ Common mistakes:

  • Drawing them flat or short — they must look like fingers.

4. Ruminant and bird digestion

🏷️ Labels to include:
Oesophagus Rumen Small intestine Gizzard Stomach Intestine

✏️ Steps to draw it:
  1. A labelled flow diagram (boxes and arrows) is acceptable.
  2. Cow: show the arrow from rumen BACK to mouth (rumination).
  3. Bird: stomach → gizzard → intestine; note grit grinds food.

❌ Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting that the cud comes back to the mouth.

5. Human respiratory system

🏷️ Labels to include:
Nostrils Windpipe Right lung Left lung Alveoli Rib cage Diaphragm

✏️ Steps to draw it:
  1. Draw the windpipe as a tube with ring lines down the middle of the chest.
  2. Split it into two branches at the bottom.
  3. Draw two large lungs, one each side (the left lung a little smaller to make room for the heart).
  4. Draw curved lines across for the ribs.
  5. Draw a dome-shaped curve under the lungs = diaphragm.
  6. Draw a circle zoom-in on the side with a bunch of tiny balloons = alveoli.
  7. Label and title.

❌ Common mistakes:

  • Drawing the diaphragm above the lungs or as a straight line (it is a dome under the lungs).
  • Forgetting the alveoli zoom-in.

6. Mechanism of breathing

🏷️ Labels to include:
Ribs move up and out / down and in Diaphragm moves down / up Air drawn in / forced out

✏️ Steps to draw it:
  1. Draw TWO diagrams side by side: (a) inhalation (b) exhalation.
  2. (a) Flatter, lower diaphragm; outward arrows on ribs; arrow INTO the windpipe.
  3. (b) Dome raised up; inward arrows on ribs; arrow OUT of the windpipe.
  4. Write a one-line caption under each.

❌ Common mistakes:

  • Mixing up which way the diaphragm moves.
  • Only drawing one stage.

7. Gas exchange in the alveoli

🏷️ Labels to include:
Alveolus Blood vessel (capillary) Oxygen Carbon dioxide

✏️ Steps to draw it:
  1. Draw one big circle = alveolus with a tube entering it.
  2. Draw a curved red blood vessel hugging its side.
  3. Arrow labelled O₂ from the alveolus into the blood.
  4. Arrow labelled CO₂ from the blood into the alveolus.

❌ Common mistakes:

  • Drawing the arrows the wrong way round.

8. Breathing model

🏷️ Labels to include:
Bottle (chest) Y-tube (windpipe) Balloons (lungs) Rubber sheet (diaphragm)

✏️ Steps to draw it:

❌ Common mistakes:

🌱 Life Processes in Plants

27. Photosynthesis

🏷️ Labels to include:
Sunlight Leaf (chlorophyll) Carbon dioxide in Water + minerals in Oxygen out Glucose/starch

✏️ Steps to draw it:
  1. Draw a large leaf with a midrib and a stalk.

  4. Arrow OUT of the leaf: oxygen.

❌ Common mistakes:

  4. Label.

❌ Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting the pore between the guard cells.

🫀 Life processes — the big picture

Five life processes keep animals alive: nutrition, respiration, circulation, excretion and reproduction. We can survive about a week without food, a day or two without water, but only a few minutes without breathing.

Number to rememberValue
Small intestine (longest part)almost 6 m — about twice the height of a classroom
Large intestineabout 1.5 m (shorter but wider)
Oxygen in inhaled / exhaled airabout 21% / about 16–17%
Carbon dioxide in inhaled / exhaled airabout 0.04% / about 4–5%
Time a cow spends chewing the cudabout 8 hours a day

🍎 Digestive system (nutrition) — in the order food travels

PartIts role (what it does)Exam key words
Mouth (buccal cavity)Food is taken in (ingestion). Teeth, tongue and saliva start digestion here.ingestion; digestion starts
TeethCut, tear, crush and grind food into small pieces — mechanical digestion; bigger surface area for juices.chew, crush, grind
TongueMixes chewed food with saliva, helps us taste, and pushes food back towards the food pipe for swallowing.mixes, tastes, swallows
Salivary glands / salivaSaliva moistens food so it is easy to swallow, and starts breaking starch → simple sugar (why chewed chapati tastes sweet).starch → sugar
Oesophagus (food pipe)Carries food from mouth to stomach by wave-like contractions and relaxations of its wall (peristalsis). No digestion here.peristalsis; carries food
StomachThick muscular bag that churns food. Its wall releases: digestive juice (breaks down proteins), acid (kills harmful bacteria) and mucus (protects the stomach lining from the acid). Food becomes a semi-liquid mass.churns; proteins; acid kills bacteria; mucus protects
LiverLargest gland. Makes bile, which neutralises the acid coming from the stomach and breaks fats into tiny droplets.bile; fats → droplets
Gall bladderStores the bile made by the liver and releases it into the small intestine.stores bile
PancreasMakes pancreatic juice, which is basic (neutralises acid) and digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats.basic juice; digests all 3
Small intestineLongest part (~6 m), coiled. Its own juices complete digestion. Digested food is absorbed through its walls into the blood.digestion completed; absorption
Villi (finger-like projections)Line the inside of the small intestine and give a huge surface area so nutrients pass quickly into blood vessels.increase surface area
Large intestine~1.5 m, wider. Absorbs most of the remaining water and some salts, turning waste into semi-solid stool. Helpful bacteria live here.absorbs water & salts
RectumStores the stool (faeces) until it is removed.stores waste
AnusOpening through which stool leaves the body — egestion.egestion
Order to memorise: Mouth → Oesophagus → Stomach → Small intestine → Large intestine → Rectum → Anus. Liver, gall bladder and pancreas add juices but food does NOT pass through them. Steps of nutrition: ingestion → digestion → absorption → assimilation → egestion.

🫁 Respiratory system (breathing & respiration)

PartIts role (what it does)Exam key words
NostrilsOpenings where air enters and leaves the body.air in/out

Breathing vs respiration

BreathingRespiration
Moving air into and out of the lungsUsing oxygen to break down glucose in cells to release energy
Physical processChemical process
Happens in the lungs/airwaysHappens in every cell
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

After exercise we breathe faster because our muscles need more energy, so more oxygen is needed and more carbon dioxide has to be removed.

✅ Quick check: every organ

1. Which organ makes bile, and what are bile's two jobs?

The liver. Bile neutralises the acid from the stomach and breaks fats into tiny droplets.

2. Why doesn't the acid in the stomach damage its own wall?

The stomach wall releases mucus, which protects the lining.

3. Name the three things the stomach wall releases and the job of each.

Digestive juice (breaks down proteins), acid (kills harmful bacteria), mucus (protects the lining).

4. What does the pancreatic juice do?

It is basic, neutralises acid, and digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

5. What is the role of the diaphragm?

It moves down to make the chest space bigger (air rushes in) and up to make it smaller (air is pushed out).

6. Why do we sneeze when we breathe in dusty air?

Hairs and mucus in the nose trap dust; the irritation makes us sneeze to throw it out, keeping dust from the lungs.

7. Why are there millions of alveoli and villi?

Both give a very large surface area — alveoli for gas exchange, villi for absorbing digested food.

8. Where is water absorbed from undigested food?

In the large intestine (with some salts).

9. How does a bird digest food without teeth?

Its muscular gizzard grinds food, helped by small stones (grit) it swallows.

10. Breathing or respiration — which is a chemical process?

Respiration (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy). Breathing is physical.

📌 Just for knowledge: this tab is not for the exam. For the exam you only need: teeth chew and crush food (mechanical digestion) — see the 🫀 Every Organ tab.

🦷 Teeth and oral health

  • Incisors (8) cut and bite · Canines (4) tear · Premolars (8) crush · Molars (12) grind.
  • We get two sets: milk teeth (20, which fall out from about age 6–8) and permanent teeth (32).
  • Tooth decay: bacteria feed on sugar left in the mouth and make acids that dissolve the hard enamel.
  • Good habits: brush twice a day with (basic) toothpaste, floss, rinse after meals, and limit sweets and fizzy drinks.

📽️ Revision slideshow: Understanding Weather (14 slides)

1. Weather and climate: what's the difference?

The atmosphere is the blanket of air around the Earth. Its condition changes all the time. Sometimes it is hot and sunny, sometimes cloudy and windy, sometimes stormy.

Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time: temperature, air pressure, wind, humidity, clouds and rain. It can change from hour to hour and day to day. "It is 38 °C and humid in Dubai this afternoon" is a statement about weather.

Climate is the average weather of a large area, worked out over a long period, usually 30 years or more. "Dubai has a hot desert climate with very little rain" is a statement about climate.

WeatherClimate
Day-to-day condition of the atmosphereAverage weather over many years (30+)
Small area, short timeLarge area, long time
Changes quickly, even within a dayStays almost the same for years
Example: "It rained heavily in Mumbai today."Example: "Mumbai has heavy rain every June–September."
Memory trick: Climate is what you expect. Weather is what you get.

The study of weather is called meteorology, and the scientists are meteorologists. In India, the India Meteorological Department (IMD), set up in 1875 with its headquarters in New Delhi, records the weather and makes forecasts.

1b. Layers of the atmosphere — where does weather happen?

The atmosphere is the blanket of air around the Earth, held by gravity. It is made of nitrogen (78%), oxygen (21%), argon (0.9%), and small amounts of carbon dioxide (about 0.04%), water vapour and dust. It is divided into five layers by how temperature changes with height:

LayerHeight (approx.)Key facts
Troposphere 🌦️0 to about 13 km (about 8 km at the poles, 18 km at the equator)All weather happens here: clouds, rain, wind, storms. It holds almost all the water vapour and dust and about three-quarters of the air. Temperature falls about 6.5 °C for every 1 km you go up. The top is called the tropopause.
Stratosphere ✈️up to about 50 kmContains the ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. Almost no clouds or weather, so the air is calm; jet planes fly in its lower part. Temperature rises with height (ozone absorbs heat).
Mesosphere ☄️50 to about 80 kmThe coldest layer (down to about −90 °C). Meteors burn up here, which we see as "shooting stars".
Thermosphere 📡80 to about 600 kmTemperature rises very high. Contains the ionosphere, which reflects radio waves back to Earth. The auroras (northern lights) happen here; the International Space Station orbits in it.
Exosphere 🛰️above about 600 kmThe outermost layer; the air is extremely thin and slowly fades into space. Many satellites orbit here.
Memory trick (from the ground up): "The Strong Man Throws Eggs" → Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere.
Q: Why does weather occur only in the troposphere?

Because the troposphere contains almost all the atmosphere's water vapour and dust (needed for clouds and rain), and it is heated from below by the ground, which makes air rise, cool and form clouds and winds. Layers above are too dry and too stable.

2. The elements of weather

Weather is made up of several elements. Each one can be measured with an instrument:

ElementWhat it meansInstrumentUnit
TemperatureHow hot or cold the air isThermometer (Six's maximum–minimum thermometer)°C or °F
Air pressureWeight of the air pressing down on the EarthBarometermillibars (mb)
Wind directionWhere the wind is coming FROMWind vaneN, S, E, W…
Wind speedHow fast the air movesAnemometerkm/h or knots
HumidityAmount of water vapour in the airHygrometer (wet-and-dry bulb)%
RainfallAmount of rain that fallsRain gaugemm or cm
SunshineHours of bright sunshineSunshine recorderhours

3. Temperature

The Sun is the main source of heat for the Earth. The energy that reaches the Earth from the Sun is called insolation (incoming solar radiation).

The air is not heated directly by the Sun's rays passing through it. The rays first heat the ground, and the ground then heats the air touching it, a bit like a hot pan heating the air above it. That's why the air near the ground is warmer than the air higher up.

Factors that affect temperature

  1. Latitude (distance from the equator): Near the equator the Sun's rays fall almost vertically, so their heat is concentrated on a small area and it is hot. Towards the poles the rays fall at a slant and spread over a larger area, so it is colder.
  2. Altitude (height above sea level): Temperature falls by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m of height. This is called the normal lapse rate. Hill stations like Shimla, Mussoorie, Darjeeling and Ooty are cool even in summer.
  3. Distance from the sea: Land heats and cools quickly, but water heats and cools slowly. Places near the sea have a moderate (equable) climate: Mumbai is never extremely hot or cold. Places far inland have an extreme (continental) climate: Delhi is very hot in summer and cold in winter.
  4. Cloud cover: Clouds block sunlight by day, so cloudy days are cooler. At night they act like a blanket and stop heat escaping, so cloudy nights are warmer. Deserts have clear skies, which is why they are very hot by day and cold at night.
  5. Winds and ocean currents: Warm winds and currents raise temperature, and cold ones lower it.

Working with temperature

Daily (diurnal) range = Maximum temperature − Minimum temperature
Mean daily temperature = (Maximum + Minimum) ÷ 2
°F = (°C × 9/5) + 32
Worked example: In Jaisalmer one day, the maximum is 44 °C and the minimum is 26 °C.
Daily range = 44 − 26 = 18 °C. Mean daily temperature = (44 + 26) ÷ 2 = 35 °C.
In Mumbai the same day the max might be 33 °C and min 27 °C, a range of only 6 °C, because the sea keeps the temperature moderate.

A Six's maximum–minimum thermometer records the highest and lowest temperatures of the day. Thermometers are kept in a Stevenson screen so that direct sunlight does not give a false (too high) reading.

4. Air pressure

Air has weight. The weight of the column of air pressing down on a unit area of the Earth's surface is called air pressure (atmospheric pressure). It is measured with a barometer in millibars (mb). Average pressure at sea level is about 1,013 mb.

  • Pressure falls with height. Higher up there is less air above you, so the air is "thin". Mountaineers carry oxygen cylinders, and water boils below 100 °C on high mountains, so food takes longer to cook.
  • Temperature and pressure are linked. When air is heated, it expands, becomes light and rises, creating low pressure (L). When air cools, it becomes dense and heavy and sinks, creating high pressure (H).
  • Low pressure usually brings clouds, wind and rain (rising air cools and forms clouds). High pressure usually brings clear, calm, dry weather.

On weather maps, lines joining places with the same pressure are called isobars.

5. Wind

Wind is moving air. It always blows from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure. The bigger the difference in pressure, the stronger the wind.

Naming winds: A wind is named after the direction it comes FROM. A "west wind" (westerly) blows from the west towards the east. A wind vane's arrow points towards the direction the wind is coming from.

Types of winds

  1. Permanent (planetary) winds blow in the same direction all year: the trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.
  2. Seasonal winds change direction with the season. The most important example is the monsoon winds of India (see Climate of India).
  3. Local winds blow over a small area for a short time:
    • Loo: a hot, dry, dusty wind that blows in the afternoons over north and north-west India in May and June. It can cause heatstroke.
    • Land and sea breezes blow daily along coasts.

Land breeze and sea breeze

By day, land heats faster than the sea. Air over the land rises (low pressure), and cooler air from the sea (high pressure) blows in to replace it. This is the sea breeze, which keeps coastal cities like Mumbai and Chennai pleasant in the afternoon.

At night, land cools faster than the sea. Now the sea is warmer (low pressure) and the cooler land air (high pressure) blows out to sea. This is the land breeze. Fishermen traditionally sail out early in the morning with the land breeze and return in the afternoon with the sea breeze.

Cyclones are violent storms that form around a centre of very low pressure over warm seas. Winds spiral inwards at great speed, anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere, bringing heavy rain and storm surges. The Bay of Bengal coast (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal) is often hit by cyclones.

6. Humidity

Water from seas, lakes, rivers and plants evaporates and enters the air as invisible water vapour. The amount of water vapour in the air is called humidity.

  • Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
  • Relative humidity compares how much vapour the air has with the maximum it could hold at that temperature, shown as a percentage. 100% means the air is saturated (completely full).
  • When the humidity is high, sweat does not evaporate easily from our skin, so we feel sticky and uncomfortable. That's why a humid 35 °C day in Mumbai or Dubai feels worse than a dry 35 °C day in Delhi.
  • Humidity is measured with a hygrometer. The wet-and-dry bulb type has two thermometers: one dry, one wrapped in wet cloth. The bigger the difference between them, the drier the air.

When moist air cools, it can no longer hold all its water vapour. The vapour turns into tiny water droplets. This is condensation. The temperature at which this happens is the dew point. Condensation forms dew (on grass), fog and mist (near the ground), frost (when below 0 °C) and clouds (high in the sky).

7. Clouds

A cloud is a mass of tiny water droplets or ice crystals formed when water vapour condenses around tiny particles of dust or smoke high in the air.

CloudLooks likeWeather
CirrusHigh, thin, white, feathery (ice crystals)Fair weather
CumulusPuffy, white "cotton-wool" heaps with flat basesFair weather; can grow into storm clouds
StratusLow, grey, flat layers covering the skyDull, overcast; drizzle
Nimbus (nimbostratus, cumulonimbus)Dark grey, thick; cumulonimbus are huge and tower upwardRain; cumulonimbus bring thunderstorms, lightning, hail

8. Precipitation and types of rainfall

When cloud droplets join together and become too heavy to stay in the air, they fall as precipitation: rain, snow, sleet (rain and snow mixed) or hail (balls of ice). Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge.

For rain to form, moist air must rise and cool. There are three ways air can be made to rise, giving three types of rainfall:

  1. Convectional rainfall: The Sun heats the ground strongly. The air above becomes hot and rises in currents (convection currents). As it rises it cools, condenses and forms tall cumulonimbus clouds, giving heavy rain with thunder, usually in the afternoon. Common in equatorial regions every day, and in India in the hot season (pre-monsoon storms).
  2. Orographic (relief) rainfall: Moist winds blowing from the sea meet a mountain range and are forced to rise. They cool and give heavy rain on the side facing the wind, the windward side. By the time the air crosses the mountains and sinks down the other side, it has lost its moisture and is warming up, so the far side, the leeward side, gets little rain. This dry area is called a rain-shadow area.
    Best Indian example: The Western Ghats. Mumbai (windward) gets about 240 cm of rain a year. Pune (leeward, only about 150 km away) gets only about 70 cm. Most of India's monsoon rain is orographic.
  3. Cyclonic (frontal) rainfall: When a warm, moist air mass meets a cold air mass, the lighter warm air is pushed up over the heavier cold air. It cools and gives rain. In India, the western disturbances that bring winter rain to Punjab and Haryana, and cyclones from the Bay of Bengal, give this type of rain.

9. Measuring and forecasting the weather

A weather station is a place where weather instruments are kept and readings are taken at fixed times every day. Thermometers and the hygrometer are kept inside a Stevenson screen:

  • It is a white wooden box. White reflects sunlight so the box doesn't heat up.
  • It has louvres (slatted sides) so air can flow through freely.
  • It stands on legs about 1.2 m above the ground so heat from the ground doesn't affect the reading.
  • Its door faces north in the northern hemisphere so the Sun never shines directly on the instruments when it is opened.

The rain gauge, wind vane and anemometer are kept in the open. Today, weather is also tracked by satellites (such as India's INSAT series), weather radars and weather balloons. Computers use all this data to make weather forecasts.

Why weather forecasts matter

  • Farmers decide when to sow, water and harvest.
  • Fishermen are warned not to go to sea when a cyclone is coming.
  • Pilots and ships plan safe routes.
  • Disaster management: early cyclone warnings let authorities evacuate people. When Cyclone Phailin hit Odisha in 2013, nearly a million people were moved to safety in advance, saving many lives.
  • Everyday planning: sports matches, school trips, travel.

10. Weather instruments at a glance

InstrumentMeasuresUnitHow it helps
Thermometer / maximum–minimum thermometerTemperature (highest and lowest of the day)°CDaily range, heatwave and cold-wave warnings
BarometerAir pressuremillibars (mb) / hPaFalling pressure → clouds, rain, storms; rising pressure → clear, settled weather
Rain gaugeRainfallmm / cmFlood and drought warnings, planning for farmers
Wind vaneWind directionN, NE, E…Tells which way storms and monsoon winds are coming from (named after where the wind comes from)
AnemometerWind speedkm/hCyclone and storm warnings for fishermen, ports and airports
Hygrometer (wet-and-dry bulb)Humidity%High humidity + heat → feels hotter, chance of rain
Satellites, radar, weather balloonsClouds, storms, upper-air conditions—Track cyclones days in advance; feed computer forecasts

11. Reading a weather forecast

A weather forecast is a prediction of the weather for the coming hours or days, made by meteorologists using instrument readings, satellite images and computer models.

DaySkyMax / MinChance of rainWindHumidity
Mon☀️ Sunny42 °C / 30 °C0%NW 15 km/h25%
Tue⛅ Partly cloudy39 °C / 29 °C20%W 20 km/h45%
Wed⛈️ Thunderstorms33 °C / 26 °C80%SW 45 km/h85%
Q1. Which day is best for a school trip outdoors, and which day is riskiest? Why?

Tuesday is best (not as hot as Monday, low chance of rain). Wednesday is riskiest: 80% chance of thunderstorms, strong winds of 45 km/h.

Q2. Calculate Monday's daily range of temperature.

42 − 30 = 12 °C.

Q3. What change in pressure would the barometer probably show before Wednesday? Explain.

Pressure would fall, because low pressure is linked with rising moist air, clouds and storms. Humidity also rises from 25% to 85%.

IMD colour-coded warnings

ColourMeaning
🟢 GreenNo warning — no action needed
🟡 YellowBe aware — watch for updates
🟠 OrangeBe prepared — severe weather likely
🔴 RedTake action — dangerous weather, follow official instructions

The UAE's National Centre of Meteorology (NCM) uses a similar colour system for fog, dust and rain alerts.

12. Extreme weather events

EventWhat it isEffectsExample
🌀 Tropical cycloneA huge low-pressure storm over warm seas with very strong spiralling winds and heavy rain. In India they come mainly in May and October–November, mostly from the Bay of Bengal.Storm surge floods coasts, houses and crops destroyed, power cutCyclone Phailin (Odisha, 2013); Cyclone Biparjoy (Gujarat, 2023)
🔥 HeatwaveA period of abnormally high temperatures. IMD declares one when plains reach 40 °C or more and it is well above normal, or 45 °C or more.Heatstroke, deaths, water shortages, crop and power stressNorth India, May 2024 (around 50 °C in Rajasthan)
🥶 Cold waveAbnormally low temperatures in winter, often with dense fog in the northern plainsHealth risks for the homeless and elderly, flights and trains delayedNorth India in December–January
🌊 FloodLand normally dry is covered with water after very heavy rain or overflowing riversLoss of life, homes, crops; disease spreadsKerala (2018); Assam almost every year
🏜️ DroughtA long period with much less rain than normalCrop failure, food and water shortage, farmers' debtMaharashtra, Rajasthan in weak monsoon years
