☁️ CloudburstExtremely heavy rain (100 mm or more in an hour) over a small area, usually in mountainsFlash floods and landslidesKedarnath, Uttarakhand (2013)
Staying safe: follow forecasts and warnings, move to cyclone shelters when told, drink water and stay indoors at midday in heatwaves, avoid rivers and low areas in floods, stay away from trees and open fields in lightning.

✅ Quick check: Understanding Weather

1. Why is the air near the ground warmer than the air higher up?

Because the Sun's rays heat the ground first, and the ground then heats the air in contact with it. Air farther from the ground gets less heat.

2. A place at 2,000 m has a temperature of 15 °C. Estimate the temperature at sea level nearby.

Temperature falls about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, so 2,000 m means about 13 °C less. Sea level ≈ 15 + 13 = 28 °C.

3. Why do deserts have such a large daily range of temperature?

Clear skies and dry sand: by day nothing blocks the Sun, so the sand heats quickly; at night there are no clouds to trap the heat, so it escapes quickly and the temperature drops sharply.

4. Explain why Pune gets much less rain than Mumbai.

Mumbai is on the windward side of the Western Ghats, where moist monsoon winds rise, cool and drop heavy rain. Pune is on the leeward side, in the rain shadow; the air reaching it has lost most of its moisture and is sinking and warming, so there is little rain.

5. Name the instrument and unit for: wind speed, humidity, air pressure.

Wind speed: anemometer (km/h). Humidity: hygrometer (%). Air pressure: barometer (millibars).

📽️ Revision slideshow: Climate of India (14 slides)

1. India's climate: tropical monsoon

India has a tropical monsoon type of climate. The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word mausim, meaning season. Monsoon winds are winds that reverse their direction with the seasons:

  • In summer they blow from the sea to the land (south-west monsoon), bringing heavy rain.
  • In winter they blow from the land to the sea (north-east monsoon), and are mostly dry.

India is a very large country, so its climate varies a lot from place to place. In summer, western Rajasthan can reach 48–50 °C while Pahalgam in Kashmir is about 20 °C. In winter, Drass in Ladakh can drop to −40 °C while Thiruvananthapuram is about 25 °C. Mawsynram in Meghalaya gets about 1,180 cm of rain a year, while Jaisalmer gets only about 20 cm. Even so, the monsoon gives the whole country a common rhythm of seasons.

1b. Weather, seasons and climate — what's the difference?

BasisWeatherSeasonClimate
MeaningCondition of the atmosphere at a place at a particular timeA part of the year with a typical type of weatherAverage weather of a place over a long period (30+ years)
TimeHours / daysA few monthsMany years
Changes?Changes quickly, even within a dayChanges 4 times a year in IndiaChanges very slowly
Example"It is raining in Mumbai today.""Mumbai gets heavy rain from June to September.""Mumbai has a hot, humid tropical monsoon climate."

1c. The main types of climate in India

India is one country, but because of its size and relief it has several climate types:

Climate typeFeaturesExamples (where)
Tropical wet (monsoon)Hot all year, very heavy rain (over 200 cm), short dry season; dense evergreen forestsWestern Ghats coast (Kerala, Konkan, Goa), north-east India (Meghalaya), Andaman & Nicobar Islands
Tropical wet and dry (savanna)Hot; rain in summer monsoon, long dry winter; grasslands and deciduous forestsMost of the Peninsular plateau: Maharashtra, Telangana, Odisha interior, Jharkhand
Semi-arid (steppe)Low rain (about 25–60 cm), hot summers; thorny scrubRain-shadow Deccan (interior Karnataka, Maharashtra), parts of Gujarat, Punjab–Haryana–east Rajasthan
Hot desert (arid)Very little rain (under 25 cm), very hot days, cool nights, huge daily rangeWestern Rajasthan – the Thar (Jaisalmer, Barmer)
Humid subtropicalHot, humid summers with monsoon rain; cool, dry winters with fogNorthern plains: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal plains, Delhi
Mountain (alpine) climateCool to cold; temperature falls with height; snow in winter. Ladakh is a cold desert (very dry and cold)Himalayas: Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim; Ladakh
Exam tip: "Describe the main types of climate with examples" → give the name + 2 features + 1–2 places for each type.

2. Factors that control India's climate

  1. Latitude: The Tropic of Cancer (23½° N) passes through the middle of India. The southern part lies in the tropical zone (hot most of the year). The northern part lies in the sub-tropical/temperate zone (hot summers, cold winters).
  2. The Himalayas: The high mountains in the north work like a giant wall.
    • In winter they block the freezing winds from Central Asia, so north India is not as cold as places like Mongolia at a similar latitude.
    • In summer they trap the monsoon winds, forcing them to drop their rain inside India.
  3. Altitude: Places at a height are cooler. Shimla, Darjeeling, Ooty and Munnar are hill stations.
  4. Distance from the sea: Coastal places like Mumbai, Chennai and Kochi have an equable (moderate) climate. Interior places like Delhi, Kanpur and Amritsar have an extreme (continental) climate with a big difference between summer and winter.
  5. Relief (mountains): Mountains decide where rain falls. The windward slopes of the Western Ghats get heavy rain, while the leeward Deccan Plateau is a rain-shadow area.
  6. Pressure and winds: Changes in air pressure over the land and sea cause the monsoon winds to reverse. Western disturbances (low-pressure systems from the Mediterranean region) bring winter rain to north-west India, carried by the westerly jet stream.
Equable vs extreme: Chennai's average temperature goes from about 25 °C in January to about 33 °C in May, a range of about 8 °C. Delhi goes from about 14 °C in January to about 34 °C in June, a range of about 20 °C. The sea keeps Chennai's climate moderate.

3. The four seasons of India

The India Meteorological Department divides the year into four seasons:

❄️ (a) The cold weather season (winter): December to February

  • The Sun is overhead in the southern hemisphere, so north India receives slanting rays and becomes cold.
  • Temperature falls from south to north. January averages about 10–15 °C in the northern plains but about 24–25 °C in Chennai. Frost occurs in the north, and the Himalayas get snow. Dense fog often covers the northern plains, delaying trains and flights.
  • Skies are mostly clear, days are pleasant and sunny, nights are cold, and humidity is low.
  • Winds are the north-east trade winds, which blow from land to sea, so most of India stays dry.
  • Exception 1, Tamil Nadu coast: These winds cross the Bay of Bengal and pick up moisture, so they give winter rain to the Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu).
  • Exception 2, north-west India: Western disturbances bring light winter rain to Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and western Uttar Pradesh, and snow to the hills. This rain is called mahawat. Though small, it is very useful for rabi crops like wheat.

☀️ (b) The hot weather season (summer): March to May

  • The Sun moves north towards the Tropic of Cancer, so temperatures rise steadily. By May, north-west India reaches 45 °C or more. India's highest recorded temperature, 51 °C, was at Phalodi in Rajasthan (2016).
  • South India is less hot because of the sea's moderating effect.
  • Intense heat creates a low-pressure area over north-west India. This is very important because it later pulls in the monsoon winds.
  • Loo: strong, hot, dry winds blow in the afternoons over the northern plains, and dust storms are common in Rajasthan.
  • Pre-monsoon showers (convectional thunderstorms):
    • Mango showers: in Kerala and Karnataka, they help mangoes ripen early.
    • Blossom showers: in Kerala and nearby areas, they make coffee plants flower.
    • Kalbaisakhi (Nor'westers): violent evening thunderstorms in West Bengal and Assam. They are useful for tea, jute and rice.

🌧️ (c) The south-west monsoon season (rainy season): June to September

How it starts: In early summer a strong low-pressure area forms over north-west India. The south-east trade winds of the southern hemisphere are pulled towards it. When they cross the equator they turn right (because of the Earth's rotation) and become south-west winds. They have travelled thousands of kilometres over the warm Indian Ocean, so they are full of moisture. These are the south-west monsoon winds.

Onset: The monsoon reaches the Kerala coast around 1 June. It arrives suddenly with thunder, lightning and very heavy rain. This is called the "burst of the monsoon". It reaches Mumbai and Kolkata around 10–11 June, Delhi around the end of June, and covers the whole country by early July.

As the winds approach India, they split into two branches:

  1. Arabian Sea branch:
    • Strikes the Western Ghats. The windward western slopes and the west coast get very heavy rain (over 250 cm in places).
    • The Deccan Plateau, on the leeward side, gets much less: a rain-shadow area.
    • Part of this branch moves north along the Gujarat coast into Rajasthan, but gives very little rain there. The Aravalli hills run parallel to the wind direction, so nothing forces the air to rise. That's a major reason for the Thar Desert.
  2. Bay of Bengal branch:
    • Moves north-east towards Myanmar and north-east India. The funnel-shaped Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya force the moist air up sharply, so Mawsynram (about 1,180 cm a year) and Cherrapunji (Sohra) are among the wettest places on Earth.
    • The Himalayas block this branch and turn it westward along the Ganga plains.
    • Rainfall decreases from east to west along the plains as the winds lose moisture: Kolkata about 160 cm, Patna about 110 cm, Prayagraj about 90 cm, Delhi about 75 cm.

The two branches meet over the north-western plains around Delhi.

  • Breaks in the monsoon: The rain does not fall every day. There can be dry spells of one or two weeks in between, which can harm crops.
  • Uneven and uncertain: Some years bring floods (in Assam and Bihar, for example), others bring drought. The monsoon may also arrive late or withdraw early.
  • India gets about 75% or more of its yearly rain in this season. Kharif crops such as rice, cotton, jute, sugarcane and maize depend on it.
  • Tamil Nadu stays fairly dry in this season. It lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats for the Arabian Sea branch, and the Bay branch blows parallel to its coast.

🍂 (d) The retreating (post-) monsoon season: October and November

  • The Sun moves south and the low pressure over north India weakens, so the monsoon winds weaken and withdraw, starting from north-west India in September.
  • Skies clear, but the ground is still wet, so it is hot and humid for a while. This is called "October heat".
  • The low pressure moves to the Bay of Bengal, where tropical cyclones often form and strike the east coast (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu), causing great damage.
  • The retreating monsoon and the north-east monsoon winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and give heavy rain to the Coromandel coast. Chennai gets most of its rain in October–December, unlike Mumbai, which gets most of its rain in July.
Reading a climate graph: Bars show rainfall and the line shows temperature. Look for (1) the wettest months, (2) the hottest month, (3) the temperature range. Mumbai's July peak shows it gets SW monsoon rain. Chennai's November peak shows it gets NE / retreating monsoon rain. Chennai's temperature line is flatter than Delhi's would be, which shows an equable climate.

4. Distribution of rainfall

RainfallAreas
Very high (over 200 cm)West coast and windward Western Ghats; north-east India (Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal); sub-Himalayan West Bengal; Andaman & Nicobar Islands
High (100–200 cm)Eastern India: West Bengal, Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, eastern Madhya Pradesh, Bihar; foothills of the Himalayas
Moderate (60–100 cm)Uttar Pradesh, most of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, eastern Gujarat, Kashmir
Low (20–60 cm)Punjab, Haryana, eastern Rajasthan, Kutch, and the rain-shadow interior of Karnataka and Maharashtra
Very low (under 20 cm)Western Rajasthan (Thar Desert) and Ladakh (Leh gets only about 10 cm, as it lies beyond the Himalayas)
Two rules to remember: (1) Rainfall generally decreases from east to west in north India and from the coast towards the interior. (2) Areas with low rainfall also have the most unreliable rainfall, so they suffer droughts more often.

5. The monsoon as a unifying force

Although India's climate varies a lot, the monsoon ties the whole country together:

  • Farmers across India plan sowing and harvesting around its arrival. About half of India's farmland depends on rain alone.
  • Harvest festivals follow the seasons: Pongal, Onam, Bihu, Baisakhi, Makar Sankranti.
  • Rivers, reservoirs and groundwater are refilled, which supports drinking water and hydroelectricity.
  • A good monsoon helps the whole economy. A weak one causes drought, food shortages and higher prices.

6. Role of the monsoon in India's life and economy

The south-west monsoon (June–September) gives India about three-quarters of its yearly rainfall. That is why it is often called the "real finance minister of India".

AreaRole of the monsoon
🌾 AgricultureNearly half of Indians work in farming and much farmland is rain-fed. Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon (June–July) and harvested in September–October: rice, maize, cotton, jowar, soybean, groundnut. Soil moisture left after the monsoon helps rabi crops (wheat, mustard, gram), sown in October–December.
💧 WaterFills rivers, lakes, reservoirs and wells; recharges groundwater for drinking and irrigation.
⚡ ElectricityFull reservoirs produce hydroelectricity.
🏭 Industry & pricesGood harvests give raw materials (cotton, sugarcane, jute) to industries and keep food prices low. Farmers earn more and buy more goods (tractors, bikes, phones), helping the whole economy.
🎉 CultureFestivals and harvest celebrations (Onam, Pongal, Bihu, Baisakhi), songs and art are linked to the monsoon.
⚠️ ProblemsThe monsoon is uncertain: it may arrive late, have long breaks, or bring too much rain. This causes droughts in some areas and floods in others (Assam, Bihar), damaging crops, homes and lives.
Q: Analyse how a weak monsoon affects a farmer, a city and the country.

Farmer: crops fail, income falls, debt rises. City: water shortages, food prices rise, less hydroelectricity → power cuts. Country: food may need to be imported, prices (inflation) rise, and economic growth slows.

7. Climate change — and what we can do

Climate change is the long-term change in the Earth's temperature and weather patterns. Today it is mainly caused by humans adding greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide) to the air. These gases trap heat, like the glass of a greenhouse — the greenhouse effect — so the Earth gets warmer (global warming).

Causes

  • Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) for electricity, vehicles and factories
  • Deforestation — fewer trees to absorb CO₂
  • Methane from rice fields, cattle and landfills
  • Industry and cement making

Effects on India

  • More intense and longer heatwaves
  • An erratic monsoon: more days of extreme rain and longer dry spells → floods and droughts
  • Himalayan glaciers melting, threatening rivers like the Ganga and Indus in the long run
  • Sea-level rise threatening coasts and islands (Sundarbans, Mumbai, Lakshadweep)
  • Lower crop yields, water shortages, more diseases
Key wordMeaningExamples
MitigationReducing the causes of climate change (cutting greenhouse gases)Solar and wind power, electric vehicles, public transport, planting trees, saving energy. India co-founded the International Solar Alliance (2015) and aims for net-zero emissions by 2070.
Adaptation / ResiliencePreparing for and bouncing back from climate effectsHeat action plans (Ahmedabad was first in South Asia), cyclone shelters and early warnings in Odisha, drought-resistant seeds, rainwater harvesting, mangrove planting against storm surges
SustainabilityMeeting our needs today without harming future generationsSaving water, reducing waste, recycling, using resources carefully

Global action: the Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2 °C, ideally 1.5 °C. UN SDG 13 is "Climate Action" and SDG 11 is "Sustainable Cities and Communities".

What can a student do? Switch off lights and ACs when not needed, use public transport or walk, reduce plastic, save water, plant trees, and spread awareness.
Q: Distinguish between mitigation and adaptation with one example each.

Mitigation reduces the causes of climate change, e.g. using solar power instead of coal. Adaptation reduces the harm from its effects, e.g. building cyclone shelters or a heat action plan.

✅ Quick check: Climate of India

1. Why does Rajasthan get so little rain from the Arabian Sea branch?

The Aravalli hills lie parallel to the direction of the south-west monsoon winds, so the winds are not forced to rise and cool; they pass over without giving much rain. The intense heat also makes the air hold on to its moisture.

2. Why does Chennai receive most of its rain in October–December?

During the retreating / north-east monsoon, winds blowing from the north-east cross the Bay of Bengal, pick up moisture and drop it on the Coromandel coast. In June–September, Tamil Nadu lies in a rain shadow and the Bay branch blows parallel to its coast.

3. Give two ways the Himalayas affect India's climate.

(1) They block cold winds from Central Asia in winter. (2) They trap the monsoon winds and force them to drop their rain over India, and turn the Bay branch westward along the Ganga plains.

4. What are mango showers and Kalbaisakhi?

Pre-monsoon thunderstorms in the hot season. Mango showers fall in Kerala and Karnataka and help mangoes ripen. Kalbaisakhi (Nor'westers) are violent evening storms in West Bengal and Assam, which help tea, jute and rice.

5. What is "October heat"?

After the monsoon withdraws, skies are clear and the Sun is strong, but the land is still moist. The high temperature and high humidity make the weather oppressive in October.

📽️ Revision slideshow: The Thar Desert (12 slides)

1. Location and extent

  • The Thar Desert, also called the Great Indian Desert, lies in north-west India, west of the Aravalli Range.
  • Most of it is in western Rajasthan. Small parts extend into Gujarat (up to the Rann of Kutch), Haryana and Punjab, and it continues across the border into Pakistan (Sindh and Cholistan).
  • Total area: about 2 lakh km², the largest part in India. It is one of the most densely populated deserts in the world.
  • Important towns: Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Jodhpur, Barmer.

2. Climate: why is the Thar a desert?

  • Very low rainfall: between about 10 and 50 cm a year. Most areas get under 25 cm, and Jaisalmer gets about 20 cm. Rain falls in a few heavy showers in July–August and is very unreliable: some years almost none. Rainfall increases from west to east, towards the Aravallis.
  • Extreme temperatures: Summer days can exceed 45–50 °C (Phalodi recorded 51 °C). Winter nights can drop to near 0 °C. The daily range is very large: the dry sand and clear skies heat up fast by day and lose heat fast at night.
  • Hot, dry winds (loo) and dust storms (andhi) are common in May–June.
  • Low humidity and clear skies for most of the year.

Reasons for the dry climate

  1. The Aravallis lie parallel to the Arabian Sea branch of the south-west monsoon. The winds are not forced to rise, so they pass over the region without giving much rain.
  2. The Bay of Bengal branch has already dropped most of its moisture over eastern and northern India by the time it reaches Rajasthan.
  3. The intense heat raises the air's capacity to hold moisture, so even moist air does not easily condense.
  4. There are no high mountains in the west to block and lift the winds.

3. Landforms and drainage

  • Mostly sandy plains covered with sand dunes, mounds of sand built up by the wind. Some dunes move with the wind (shifting dunes) and can bury roads and fields.
    • Barchans are crescent-shaped dunes with their "horns" pointing downwind.
    • Longitudinal dunes are long ridges lying along the direction of the wind.
  • There are also rocky areas, low hills and salt lakes (shallow lakes that dry out leaving salt), such as Sambhar Lake, the largest inland salt lake in India, on the eastern edge, and Didwana and Pachpadra.
  • The Luni is the only important river. It rises near Ajmer in the Aravallis and flows south-west into the Rann of Kutch. It is seasonal (flows mainly after rain), and its water becomes salty downstream. "Luni" comes from the Sanskrit for "salt river".
  • The Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is a huge salt marsh that floods in the monsoon and becomes a white salt desert in the dry season.

4. Natural vegetation and wildlife

Desert plants are xerophytes, plants adapted to save water:

  • Long roots reach deep groundwater. Small, thick or waxy leaves, or thorns, reduce water loss. Fleshy stems store water.
  • Common plants: khejri (Rajasthan's state tree; its pods, called sangri, are eaten), babool (acacia), ber, rohida, ker (kair) bushes, cactus, and sewan grass, a nutritious fodder.

Animals:

  • Camel: the "ship of the desert". Its hump stores fat for energy. It can go days without water and then drink a lot quickly. Wide padded feet stop it sinking into sand. Long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep out sand.
  • Great Indian Bustard: Rajasthan's state bird. A large ground bird that is critically endangered, protected in the Desert National Park near Jaisalmer and Barmer.
  • Chinkara (Indian gazelle, Rajasthan's state animal), blackbuck, desert fox, desert cat, spiny-tailed lizard, snakes, and peacocks.

5. People and their way of life

The Thar is home to many communities: Rajputs, Bishnois, Jats, Meghwals, the Rabari (Raika) camel and sheep herders, and folk musicians such as the Manganiyars and Langas. Many people live in small villages called dhanis.

The Bishnois, India's first environmentalists: Their faith forbids cutting green trees and killing animals. In 1730 at Khejarli, near Jodhpur, Amrita Devi and 363 Bishnois gave their lives hugging khejri trees to stop them being cut. This inspired the later Chipko movement. Blackbuck and chinkara still roam freely near Bishnoi villages.

Adapting to the desert

  • Houses: thick mud walls and small windows keep the inside cool by day and warm at night. Roofs are flat or conical and thatched, and walls are often whitewashed or plastered with mud and cow dung.
  • Clothes: loose, light cotton clothes. Men wear turbans (pagdi) and women cover their heads with an odhni, which protect against sun and sand. Bright colours stand out against the plain desert.
  • Food: millets like bajra (rotis), dal-baati-churma, ker-sangri; lots of milk and buttermilk.
  • Saving water: water is precious, so people harvest rainwater in tankas/kunds (covered underground tanks), johads and nadis (village ponds), and baoris (step-wells).

6. Economic activities

ActivityDetails
Animal rearingThe main occupation. Camels, sheep and goats are reared for milk, wool, leather and transport. Some herders are nomadic, moving with their animals in search of pasture.
AgricultureRain-fed crops that need little water: bajra, jowar, moth and moong beans, guar. With canal water: wheat, mustard, cotton, groundnut.
Indira Gandhi CanalOne of the longest canals in India. It starts at the Harike Barrage in Punjab (Sutlej–Beas rivers) and carries water deep into the desert towards Jaisalmer and Barmer. It has turned large areas green (Sri Ganganagar is called the "food basket of Rajasthan") and supplies drinking water. Problems: waterlogging and salty soil where too much water is used.
HandicraftsBandhani (tie-dye), mirror-work embroidery, leather goods, pottery, carpets, puppets.
TourismJaisalmer's golden fort (Sonar Qila), Sam sand dunes, camel safaris, Mehrangarh Fort (Jodhpur), the Desert Festival, the Pushkar camel fair.
Mining & energyGypsum, limestone, lignite. Oil and natural gas near Barmer. Strong sunshine and wind make it ideal for solar and wind power: the Bhadla Solar Park (Jodhpur district) is one of the largest in the world.

7. Problems and solutions

ProblemSolution
Shortage of water; droughtsRainwater harvesting (tankas, johads), canals, drip and sprinkler irrigation
Desertification: desert spreading into nearby land through overgrazing, cutting trees and moving sandPlanting shelter belts of trees, fixing dunes with grasses and shrubs, controlled grazing
Sandstorms; shifting dunes burying fields and roadsWindbreaks of trees around fields
Waterlogging and salinity in canal areasCareful use of water, drainage, salt-tolerant crops
Endangered wildlife (Great Indian Bustard)Desert National Park, breeding programmes, safer power lines

The Central Arid Zone Research Institute (CAZRI) in Jodhpur researches ways to farm and live sustainably in the desert.

✅ Quick check: Thar Desert

1. Give two reasons why the Thar Desert receives so little rain.

(1) The Aravallis lie parallel to the SW monsoon winds, so the air isn't forced to rise. (2) The Bay of Bengal branch has lost its moisture by the time it reaches Rajasthan. (Also: high heat and no mountains to the west.)

2. How is the camel adapted to life in the desert?

Hump stores fat; can survive long without water; wide padded feet for sand; long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep out sand.

3. How has the Indira Gandhi Canal changed the Thar? Mention one problem.

It brings water from the Harike Barrage (Punjab) into the desert, allowing crops like wheat, cotton and mustard and supplying drinking water. Problem: waterlogging and salinity of soil.

4. Why are houses in the Thar built with thick mud walls?

Thick mud walls are poor conductors of heat: they keep houses cool during the scorching day and warm during the cold night.

5. Who are the Bishnois and why are they famous?

A community of the Thar whose faith protects trees and animals. In 1730 at Khejarli, Amrita Devi and 363 Bishnois died protecting khejri trees.

📝 Practice sheet: 15 fresh questions on this topic

1. The Guptas and the "classical age"

  • After the Kuṣhāṇa empire weakened, new kingdoms rose. The Guptas began as regional rulers in the area of present-day Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
  • Their empire flourished from about the 3rd to the 6th century CE, with its capital at Pāṭaliputra (present-day Patna).
  • It is called the classical age (or golden age) because a long period of peace and stability let scholars, artists and scientists do outstanding work in literature, art, science and mathematics.
How do we know? From inscriptions (on pillars and copper plates), coins, literature, buildings and sculptures, and the account of the Chinese traveller Faxian. Using many sources helps avoid one-sided conclusions.

2. The Gupta rulers

RulerKey facts
Śhrī GuptaFounder of the dynasty.
Chandragupta IFirst to take the title Mahārājādhirāja ("great king of kings"). Married the Lichchhavi princess Kumāradevī — a strategic alliance; his gold coins show the king and queen together.
SamudraguptaGreat warrior king who expanded the empire. His achievements are recorded in the Prayāga praśhasti (on the Allahabad pillar), written by his court poet Hariṣheṇa, which describes his aim of dharaṇi-bandha ("binding / unifying the Earth"). He defeated many kings in the south, including the Pallava king, but gave their kingdoms back in return for tribute and loyalty. Performed the aśhvamedha yajña. His coins show him playing the veena — a patron of music and poetry.
Chandragupta II (Vikramāditya)Called "II" because an earlier king had the same name (his grandfather, Chandragupta I). Took the title Vikramāditya. Consolidated and beautified the empire. The rust-free Iron Pillar (now at Mehrauli, Delhi) belongs to his reign. Married his daughter Prabhāvatī Gupta into the Vākāṭaka family. A devotee of Viṣhṇu. Faxian visited India in his time.
Kumāragupta IRuled a long, mostly peaceful reign; the great centre of learning at Nālandā was founded around his time.
SkandaguptaDefended the empire against the Hūṇas (Huns) from Central Asia.
How the Guptas held power — 3 ways: ① military campaigns; ② matrimonial alliances (marriage ties, e.g. Kumāradevī, Prabhāvatī Gupta); ③ land grants to local rulers, priests and chieftains, recorded on copper plates. Defeated kings were often reinstated as tributaries.

Why carve achievements on pillars? To show the king's power and legitimacy to everyone, and to make the record last for future generations.

3. Governing the empire

  • Kings used grand titles such as Mahārājādhirāja and chakravartin (universal ruler) and performed the aśhvamedha yajña (horse sacrifice) to show supreme power.
  • Administration was decentralised: the empire was divided into provinces, often run by local rulers and officials.
  • Land grants (recorded on copper plates) rewarded loyalty and brought new lands under cultivation.

4. Other kingdoms of the time

KingdomRegionRemember
VākāṭakasCentral India / DeccanAllied to the Guptas by marriage. Prabhāvatī Gupta (daughter of Chandragupta II) married a Vākāṭaka prince and ruled as regent for her young sons — "mother of two kings". Ajanta's later caves date from this period.
PallavasSouth IndiaCapital Kāñchipuram, the "city of a thousand temples"; a great centre of learning (ghaṭikā).
Varmans of KāmarūpaNorth-east (Brahmaputra valley, Assam)Accepted Samudragupta's power as tributaries but kept their kingdom.

5. Life, trade and Faxian's account

  • Trade linked India with South-East Asia and the Mediterranean world (ships stopped at places like Socotra). Exports included textiles, spices and precious stones.
  • The Guptas issued many beautiful gold coins, showing wealth and fine metalwork.
  • Society included farmers, merchants, artisans and scholars; merchants and craftsmen were organised and prosperous.
Faxian (Fa-Hien), a Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled to India in Chandragupta II's time, wrote that:
✅ people were numerous, prosperous and happy; there were charity houses and free hospitals/medicines for the poor; cities were rich.
❌ but the chaṇḍālas were treated harshly — made to live outside the city and avoided by others.

Exam point: one traveller's account shows only part of the picture — compare it with other sources.

6. Science, mathematics and medicine

ScholarContribution
Āryabhaṭa (c. 500 CE, Kusumapura / Pāṭaliputra)Wrote the Āryabhaṭīya. Said the Earth spins on its axis; explained eclipses scientifically (shadows of the Earth and Moon, not demons); calculated planetary motions, the length of the year and a very accurate value of π; used the place-value number system.
Varāhamihira (Ujjayinī)Wrote the encyclopaedic Bṛihat Saṃhitā, covering astronomy, weather, plants, architecture, gems and more.
ĀyurvedaMedical knowledge was organised in texts like the Charaka Saṃhitā and Suśhruta Saṃhitā (Suśhruta is famous for surgery).
MetallurgyThe Iron Pillar at Mehrauli is over 1,600 years old and has hardly rusted — proof of advanced iron-working skill.

7. Literature, art and architecture

  • Sanskrit literature flourished. Kālidāsa, the greatest poet-playwright, wrote Abhijñāna-śhākuntalam (play), Meghadūtam ("The Cloud Messenger") and Raghuvaṃśham — full of nature and feeling. The Purāṇas were compiled.
  • Ajanta (Maharashtra): rock-cut caves with beautiful paintings of the Jātaka tales (stories of the Buddha's past lives).
  • Udayagiri (near Vidisha, MP): rock-cut caves with carvings of Hindu deities, especially Viṣhṇu (as Varāha, the boar).
  • Deogarh (UP): the Daśhāvatāra temple, one of the earliest stone temples in north India.
  • Sārnāth: graceful sculptures of the seated Buddha.
  • Kings were patrons of art, so artists, poets and scholars were supported by the court.
PlaceMatch it to
PāṭaliputraCapital of the Guptas
UjjayinīProminent centre of learning (Varāhamihira)
UdayagiriRock-cut caves with carvings of Viṣhṇu
AjantaCave paintings of the Jātaka tales
KāñchipuramPallava capital, "city of a thousand temples"

8. Decline of the empire

  • From the late 5th–6th century CE, repeated invasions by the Hūṇas (Huns) from Central Asia drained the empire.
  • Powerful regional rulers and feudatories broke away and became independent.
  • Weaker later rulers could not hold the empire together.
Legacy: the Gupta age set patterns in art, temple building, Sanskrit literature and science that later kingdoms followed. Peace and stability allowed culture and knowledge to grow.

🔑 Key terms

PraśhastiAn inscription written in praise of a king (e.g. Prayāga praśhasti by Hariṣheṇa).
Mahārājādhirāja"Great king of kings" — a title of supreme power.
ChakravartinA universal ruler.
Aśhvamedha yajñaHorse sacrifice performed by a king to show his authority.
Dharaṇi-bandha"Binding / unifying the Earth" — Samudragupta's aim.
TributaryA ruler who keeps his kingdom but pays tribute to a stronger king.
RegentSomeone who rules on behalf of a king who is too young (Prabhāvatī Gupta).
Classical ageA period of great, lasting achievements that later ages look back to.

Use a dot for cities, shading for Magadha, and add a key and title.

✅ Quick check: The Gupta Era

1. Why is the Gupta period called the "classical age"?

Because long peace and stability allowed great achievements in art, literature, science and mathematics that influenced later times.

2. Who wrote the Prayāga praśhasti and about whom?

Hariṣheṇa, the court poet, about Samudragupta.

3. Which Gupta ruler was known as Vikramāditya?

Chandragupta II.

4. Why is he called Chandragupta "II"?

Because an earlier ruler, his grandfather Chandragupta I, had the same name.

5. Name three ways the Guptas consolidated their power.

Military campaigns, matrimonial alliances, and land grants (with defeated kings kept as tributaries).

6. Who was Prabhāvatī Gupta?

Daughter of Chandragupta II who married into the Vākāṭaka family and ruled as regent for her sons.

7. Give two good and one bad thing Faxian noted.

Good: prosperous, happy people; charity houses and free medicines. Bad: harsh treatment of the chaṇḍālas.

8. Name two ideas of Āryabhaṭa.

The Earth spins on its axis; eclipses are caused by shadows of the Earth and Moon.

9. Why is the Iron Pillar famous?

It is over 1,600 years old and has hardly rusted — proof of advanced metallurgy.

10. What caused the decline of the Gupta empire?

Hūṇa invasions and powerful regional rulers breaking away.

📝 Practice sheet: 15 questions, no time limit

1. What is a constitution and why is it important?

A constitution is the supreme rulebook of a nation. It sets out how the country is governed, what powers the government has, and what rights and duties citizens have. Every law must follow it.

Why India needs it:

  • It sets up the government and says who makes, carries out and judges laws.
  • It limits power, so no leader or government can do whatever it likes.
  • It protects citizens' rights, especially minorities and weaker groups.
  • It states the country's ideals (justice, liberty, equality, fraternity) and keeps a very diverse country united.
Think of it like school rules: the rules say who is in charge (principal, teachers), what students can do (rights) and must do (duties). Even the principal must follow them. The Constitution does this for a whole country.

Facts: India's Constitution is the longest written constitution in the world. It began with 395 articles and 8 schedules and can be changed by amendments.

2. The making of the Constitution

EventDate / fact
Constituent Assembly first meets9 December 1946 (389 members; 299 after Partition in 1947)
Objectives Resolution (basis of the Preamble)Moved by Jawaharlal Nehru, 13 December 1946
Drafting Committee formed29 August 1947, chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar
Constitution adopted26 November 1949 — now celebrated as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas)
Came into force26 January 1950 — Republic Day. This date was chosen because on 26 January 1930 Congress declared Purna Swaraj (complete independence).
Time taken2 years, 11 months and 18 days

Key leaders and their contributions

LeaderContribution
Dr B.R. AmbedkarChairman of the Drafting Committee; called the "Father (chief architect) of the Indian Constitution"; fought for equality and the end of untouchability.
Dr Rajendra PrasadPresident of the Constituent Assembly; later India's first President.
Jawaharlal NehruMoved the Objectives Resolution, which became the Preamble.
Sardar Vallabhbhai PatelHeaded committees on Fundamental Rights and minorities; united the princely states.
B.N. RauConstitutional adviser; prepared the first draft.
Women members (15)e.g. Sarojini Naidu, Hansa Mehta, Durgabai Deshmukh, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur — pushed for equal rights for women.

Borrowed ideas: parliamentary system (Britain) • Fundamental Rights (USA) • Directive Principles (Ireland) • Fundamental Duties (former USSR) • federation with a strong centre (Canada). The original was handwritten in calligraphy and decorated by artists led by Nandalal Bose.

3. The Preamble — the Constitution's introduction

"WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation…"

"We, the people" shows that power comes from the people. The words socialist, secular and integrity were added in 1976 (42nd Amendment).

WordMeaningIn daily life
SovereignIndia makes its own decisions; no outside power controls itIndia chooses its own laws and foreign policy
SocialistReducing the gap between rich and poorFree mid-day meals, subsidised food
SecularThe state has no official religion and treats all religions equallyStudents of all faiths study together; all festivals respected
DemocraticPeople choose their government through electionsAdults over 18 vote; class elections for a monitor
RepublicThe head of state (President) is elected, not a kingAny citizen can become President
JusticeFairness — social, economic, politicalEveryone gets a fair hearing in a dispute
LibertyFreedom of thought, expression, belief and worshipYou can share your opinion respectfully
EqualitySame status and opportunities for allEveryone can try out for the school team
FraternityBrotherhood; respecting each other's dignityNot bullying anyone because of their background

4. The three organs of government

OrganJobAt the Union (national) levelAt the state level
🏛️ LegislatureMakes laws, passes the budget, questions the governmentParliament = President + Lok Sabha (elected by people) + Rajya Sabha (elected by state assemblies)State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha)
⚙️ ExecutiveCarries out (implements) laws and runs the countryPresident (head of state), Prime Minister and Council of Ministers (real power), civil servantsGovernor, Chief Minister and ministers
⚖️ JudiciaryInterprets laws, settles disputes, protects rightsSupreme Court (the highest court)High Courts, then district courts

Separation of powers and checks and balances: each organ has its own job and keeps a check on the others. For example, Parliament can question ministers, and the Supreme Court can strike down a law that goes against the Constitution (judicial review). The judiciary is independent so it can judge fairly.

Example: Parliament passes the Right to Education Act (legislature) → the education ministry and schools put it into practice (executive) → if a school refuses a child admission unfairly, a court can order it to follow the law (judiciary).

5. Fundamental Rights (Part III)

Basic rights guaranteed to all citizens. If they are violated, you can go to court.

RightWhat it meansExample
1. Right to EqualityEveryone is equal before the law; no discrimination by religion, caste, sex, race or place of birth; untouchability abolishedA café cannot refuse someone because of their caste
2. Right to FreedomFreedom of speech and expression, to assemble peacefully, form associations, move and live anywhere in India, and practise any profession. Includes the right to life and personal liberty, and free education for children aged 6–14Writing a letter to a newspaper criticising a policy
3. Right against ExploitationNo forced labour or human trafficking; no child under 14 may work in factories, mines or hazardous jobsA 12-year-old cannot be made to work in a firecracker factory
4. Right to Freedom of ReligionFollow, practise and spread any religionCelebrating your festival freely
5. Cultural and Educational RightsMinorities can protect their language and culture and run their own schoolsA community running a school that teaches its language
6. Right to Constitutional RemediesYou can go to the High Court or Supreme Court if your rights are violated. Dr Ambedkar called it the "heart and soul" of the ConstitutionFiling a case when denied admission unfairly
Rights have limits: freedom of speech does not allow spreading hate or lies that harm others.

6. Fundamental Duties (Article 51A)

Added in 1976 (42nd Amendment). There are now 11 duties. Rights and duties go together. Examples:

  • Respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem
  • Protect the unity and integrity of India
  • Promote harmony and brotherhood; respect the dignity of women
  • Protect the environment — forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife
  • Develop a scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry
  • Protect public property and avoid violence
  • Parents/guardians must give their children aged 6–14 the chance of education (added in 2002)

7. Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV)

Guidelines for the government to build a fair, welfare state. Unlike Fundamental Rights, they cannot be enforced in a court, but governments should follow them when making laws. Idea borrowed from Ireland.

Directive PrincipleReal example
Equal pay for equal work for men and womenEqual Remuneration laws
Right to work, education and help in old age, sickness and unemploymentMGNREGA (100 days of work), old-age pensions
Organise village panchayatsPanchayati Raj system
Early childhood care and educationAnganwadis, mid-day meals
Protect the environment, forests and wildlifeWildlife Protection Act, national parks
Promote international peaceIndia's role in UN peacekeeping

Rights vs Duties vs Directive Principles

BasisFundamental RightsFundamental DutiesDirective Principles
For whomCitizens get themCitizens must follow themGuide the government
Court?Enforceable in courtNot enforceable in courtNot enforceable in court
Borrowed fromUSAFormer USSRIreland
ExampleRight to EqualityProtect the environmentEqual pay for equal work

✅ Quick check: The Constitution

1. Why is the Constitution called the rulebook of the nation?

Because it is the supreme law: it sets up the government, divides and limits its powers, and lists citizens' rights and duties. Every law must follow it.

2. Who was the chairman of the Drafting Committee? Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly?

Dr B.R. Ambedkar • Dr Rajendra Prasad

3. Why is 26 January celebrated as Republic Day?

The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. The date was chosen to honour 26 January 1930, when Purna Swaraj (complete independence) was declared.

4. Name the three organs of government and the job of each.

Legislature – makes laws; Executive – implements laws; Judiciary – interprets laws and settles disputes.

5. A 13-year-old is working in a hotel kitchen. Which Fundamental Right is violated?

The Right against Exploitation (no child labour under 14). The child also has the right to free education (6–14).

6. How are Directive Principles different from Fundamental Rights?

Fundamental Rights can be enforced in a court; Directive Principles are guidelines for the government and cannot be enforced in court.

7. How can you apply 'fraternity' at school?

By treating everyone with respect and dignity, including classmates from different backgrounds, and never bullying or excluding anyone.

Community values and source analysis

Respect, tolerance, responsibility, cooperation and empathy only mean something when they show in how people behave. When given a source, identify its main claim, pick out evidence, explain what it suggests, and link it to a civic principle.

📽️ Revision slideshow: Maps of India (14 slides)

1. Map skills: the basics

A map is a drawing of the Earth's surface, or part of it, on a flat surface, drawn to scale. A globe shows the whole Earth correctly but is hard to carry and can't show small details. Maps can show any area in detail.

Every map has three main components:

  1. Distance (scale): the ratio between distance on the map and real distance on the ground. It can be shown three ways:
    • Statement: "1 cm represents 50 km"
    • Representative fraction (RF): 1 : 5,000,000
    • Linear (bar) scale: a line divided into marked distances
    A large-scale map shows a small area in great detail (a town plan). A small-scale map shows a big area with less detail (a map of India).
  2. Direction: Most maps have an arrow pointing North. The four cardinal directions are North, South, East and West. The four intermediate directions are North-East, South-East, South-West and North-West.
  3. Symbols: Conventional signs and colours stand for real features: blue for water, a dotted line for a boundary, a triangle for a peak. The key or legend explains them.

Types of maps

  • Physical (relief) maps show natural features: mountains, plateaus, plains, rivers, deserts, seas.
  • Political maps show countries, states, boundaries, capitals and cities.
  • Thematic maps show one theme: rainfall, crops, population, roads, minerals.
Worked example (scale): On a map with scale 1 cm = 50 km, Delhi and Jaipur are 5.4 cm apart. Real distance = 5.4 × 50 = 270 km.

2. Location and size of India

  • India lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and the Eastern Hemisphere.
  • Latitudinal extent: 8°4′ N to 37°6′ N. Longitudinal extent: 68°7′ E to 97°25′ E.
  • The Tropic of Cancer (23°30′ N) divides India into almost two equal halves. It passes through 8 states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.
  • Area: about 3.28 million km², about 2.4% of the world's land. India is the 7th largest country (after Russia, Canada, the USA, China, Brazil and Australia).
  • Population: India is now the world's most populous country (UN estimates, 2023).
  • North–South: about 3,214 km. East–West: about 2,933 km.
  • Coastline: about 7,516 km including the islands. Land border: about 15,200 km.

Extreme points

DirectionPoint
NorthernmostIndira Col (Ladakh)
Southernmost (mainland)Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin), Tamil Nadu
Southernmost (whole country)Indira Point, Great Nicobar Island
WesternmostKutch district, Gujarat
EasternmostKibithu area, Arunachal Pradesh

Indian Standard Time (IST)

From east to west, India stretches about 29° of longitude. The Earth turns 1° every 4 minutes, so the Sun rises in Arunachal Pradesh about 2 hours earlier than in Gujarat. To avoid confusion, the whole country uses one time, set by the Standard Meridian 82°30′ E, which passes through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

Fun fact for Dubai: UAE time is GMT + 4, so India is 1 hour 30 minutes ahead of Dubai. At 6:00 pm in Dubai, it is 7:30 pm in India.

India's neighbours

NeighbourDirectionIndian states / UTs on the border
PakistanNorth-westGujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh
AfghanistanNorth-westLadakh (the area under Pakistan's occupation)
ChinaNorthLadakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh
NepalNorthUttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Sikkim
BhutanNorth-eastSikkim, West Bengal, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh
BangladeshEastWest Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
MyanmarEastArunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram
Sri LankaSouth (across the sea)Separated from Tamil Nadu by the Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar
MaldivesSouth-west (across the sea)South of the Lakshadweep Islands

India is surrounded by the Arabian Sea (west), the Bay of Bengal (east) and the Indian Ocean (south). It is the only country with an ocean named after it. Its central position at the head of the Indian Ocean helps its trade with both West Asia/Africa and East Asia.

3. The physical map of India: six physical divisions

⛰️ (1) The Himalayan Mountains (north)

The Himalayas are young fold mountains stretching about 2,400 km from Jammu & Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh like an arc. They have three parallel ranges:

  • Himadri (Greater Himalayas): the highest, average height about 6,000 m, always covered in snow. Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) in Sikkim is the highest peak in the Indian Himalayas. Glaciers here (like Gangotri) are the source of rivers like the Ganga.
  • Himachal (Lesser Himalayas): 3,700–4,500 m. Famous valleys (Kashmir, Kangra, Kullu) and hill stations (Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital, Darjeeling).
  • Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas): the lowest, southernmost range, with flat valleys called duns (for example, Dehradun).

North of them lie the Trans-Himalayas (Karakoram, Ladakh and Zaskar ranges). K2 (Godwin Austen, 8,611 m) in the Karakoram is shown on Indian maps as the highest peak of India. In the east, the Himalayas turn south as the Purvanchal (Patkai, Naga, Manipur and Mizo hills).

Importance: They block cold winds, bring monsoon rain, feed perennial rivers, have forests and wildlife, attract tourists and pilgrims, and form a natural frontier.

🌾 (2) The Northern Plains

  • Formed by alluvium (fine soil) deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra and their tributaries over millions of years.
  • Very flat and fertile, with plenty of water: India's "food bowl" for wheat, rice and sugarcane. Very densely populated.
  • Divided into the Punjab plains (west, by the Indus tributaries), the Ganga plains (middle) and the Brahmaputra plains (Assam, east).
  • The Ganga–Brahmaputra delta (Sundarbans) is the largest delta in the world, home of the Royal Bengal tiger.

🏜️ (3) The Thar (Great Indian) Desert

Lies to the west of the Aravalli hills, mainly in western Rajasthan. Sandy, with dunes, very little rain (under 25 cm in most parts), and extreme temperatures. The Luni is its only significant river. (See the Thar Desert tab for full notes.)

🪨 (4) The Peninsular Plateau

  • The oldest landmass of India, made of hard ancient rocks. It was part of the old supercontinent Gondwana. Triangular in shape.
  • The Narmada river divides it into two parts:
    • Central Highlands (north of the Narmada): the Malwa Plateau, Bundelkhand and the Chota Nagpur Plateau. Chota Nagpur is very rich in minerals like coal and iron ore. Bordered by the Aravalli range (north-west, one of the oldest fold mountains in the world) and the Vindhya range.
    • Deccan Plateau (south of the Narmada): bordered by the Satpura range (north), the Western Ghats (west) and the Eastern Ghats (east). It is higher in the west and slopes gently eastward, so most rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) flow east into the Bay of Bengal. The black soil of the Deccan is excellent for cotton.
  • Western Ghats (Sahyadri): continuous, higher, cause heavy orographic rain. Anamudi (2,695 m) in Kerala is the highest peak of south India.
  • Eastern Ghats: broken into separate hills by the east-flowing rivers, and lower. The two Ghats meet in the Nilgiri Hills (Doddabetta, 2,637 m; Ooty).
  • Narmada and Tapi are the exceptions. They flow west into the Arabian Sea through rift valleys (long cracks) between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.
  • The Meghalaya Plateau in the north-east is an extension of the Peninsular Plateau.

🏖️ (5) The Coastal Plains

Western Coastal PlainEastern Coastal Plain
Between the Western Ghats and the Arabian SeaBetween the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal
NarrowWide and flat
Parts: Konkan (Mumbai–Goa), Kannad/Canara (Karnataka), Malabar (Kerala)Parts: Northern Circars (north) and Coromandel coast (south)
Short, fast rivers; no big deltas. Kerala has lagoons called backwaters (kayals).Large, fertile deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, good for rice.
Ports: Mumbai, Kandla, Mormugao (Goa), Mangaluru, KochiPorts: Kolkata, Paradip, Visakhapatnam, Chennai. Lakes: Chilika (Odisha, the largest brackish-water lagoon in India), Pulicat

🏝️ (6) The Islands

  • Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Bay of Bengal): about 570 islands, the peaks of a submerged mountain range. Thick forests. Barren Island has India's only active volcano. Capital: Sri Vijaya Puram (formerly Port Blair). Indira Point is at the southern tip of Great Nicobar.
  • Lakshadweep (Arabian Sea): 36 small coral islands (atolls). Capital: Kavaratti.

🌊 Major rivers

Himalayan riversPeninsular rivers
Perennial: fed by melting snow and rain, so they flow all yearSeasonal: mostly rain-fed, so flow drops in the dry season
Long, form large plains; good for irrigation and navigationShorter, flow over hard rock; good for hydroelectricity (waterfalls)
Indus, Ganga (about 2,525 km, the longest river in India), Yamuna, BrahmaputraMahanadi, Godavari (the largest peninsular river, "Dakshin Ganga"), Krishna, Kaveri (flow east); Narmada, Tapi (flow west)

4. The political map of India

India is a union of 28 states and 8 union territories (UTs). States have their own elected governments. Union territories are governed directly by the central government through an Administrator or Lieutenant Governor, though Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir have their own legislatures too.

✅ Quick check: Maps of India

1. Why do most peninsular rivers flow east?

The Deccan Plateau is higher in the west (Western Ghats) and slopes gently towards the east, so rivers like the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow east into the Bay of Bengal.

2. Why does India have one standard time? Which meridian is used?

India spans about 29° of longitude, a local-time difference of about 2 hours. One standard time avoids confusion. It is based on 82°30′ E, passing through Mirzapur (UP); IST = GMT + 5:30.

3. Name the 8 states that the Tropic of Cancer passes through.

Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram.

4. Give two differences between the western and eastern coastal plains.

The western plain is narrow with no large deltas; the eastern plain is wide with large fertile deltas (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri).

5. Which range separates the Central Highlands from the Deccan, and which river flows between Vindhya and Satpura?

The Narmada river (in its rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges) is the dividing line; the Satpura range forms the northern edge of the Deccan.

📝 Practice sheet: 15 fresh questions on this topic

📋 How to answer a case study

  1. Read the questions first, then read the case and underline key facts (numbers, places, causes, effects).
  2. Identify the concept from your chapter (e.g. rain shadow, Fundamental Right, cyclone, monsoon).
  3. Answer using evidence from the case + your own textbook knowledge.
  4. For "suggest / recommend" questions, give practical, specific solutions and say how each helps.
  5. Use full sentences and key terms.

Case 1 — Cyclone Biparjoy, Gujarat (June 2023)

In June 2023, a severe cyclone named Biparjoy formed over the Arabian Sea and moved slowly towards the coast of Gujarat. The India Meteorological Department tracked it for days using satellites and radar, and issued red alerts. Authorities moved over one lakh people from coastal villages in Kutch and Saurashtra to shelters before landfall near Jakhau Port on 15 June. Strong winds uprooted trees and electricity poles and heavy rain flooded low areas, but very few lives were lost.
1. What type of extreme weather event is described? Over which sea did it form?

A tropical cyclone; it formed over the Arabian Sea.

2. Which instruments/technology helped track the cyclone?

Satellites and weather radar (plus anemometers and barometers at weather stations).

3. Why were very few lives lost?

Accurate forecasts and red alerts were issued days in advance, so over a lakh people were evacuated to shelters before landfall.

4. Suggest two ways coastal communities can become more resilient to cyclones.

Build strong cyclone shelters and houses; plant mangroves as a natural barrier against storm surges; keep early-warning systems and evacuation drills.

Case 2 — Kerala floods (August 2018)

In August 2018 Kerala received far more monsoon rain than normal. Dams filled up and many had to release water at the same time. Rivers overflowed, and landslides struck the hilly districts. More than 400 people died and over a million people had to stay in relief camps. Fishermen used their boats to rescue thousands of people. Scientists warn that heavy-rain events like this are becoming more frequent as the climate warms.
1. Which season and which branch of the monsoon caused this rain?

The south-west monsoon season (June–September), Arabian Sea branch, which hits the Western Ghats and Kerala first.

2. Why does Kerala get such heavy rain?

It lies on the windward side of the Western Ghats: moist south-west monsoon winds rise, cool and drop heavy rain (relief/orographic rainfall).

3. How is this event linked to climate change?

A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so extreme rainfall events become heavier and more frequent; the monsoon becomes more erratic.

4. Recommend two measures to reduce flood damage.

Better dam management and early warnings; avoid building on floodplains and steep slopes; protect forests to reduce landslides; better drainage.

Case 3 — The Allahabad Pillar inscription (source-based)

The court poet Harishena composed a long praise poem (prashasti) in Sanskrit about Samudragupta, which was carved on an Ashokan pillar at Prayag (Allahabad). It says Samudragupta uprooted many kings of northern India and added their lands to his empire. Rulers of the south were defeated, but their kingdoms were given back to them after they accepted him as overlord. Rulers on the frontiers paid tribute, followed his orders and came to his court. The poem also praises him as a poet and a musician.
1. Who wrote this source and what kind of source is it?

Harishena, Samudragupta's court poet; it is a prashasti (praise inscription) — a primary source.

2. How did Samudragupta treat the kings of the north differently from those of the south?

Northern kings were uprooted and their lands added to the empire; southern kings surrendered and were given back their kingdoms as tributary rulers.

3. Why should historians be careful when using this source?

A prashasti was written to praise the king, so it may exaggerate his victories and leave out defeats; it should be checked with other sources (coins, other inscriptions).

4. What does the source tell us about the Gupta system of tributary rulers?

Many rulers kept their kingdoms but paid tribute, attended the court and obeyed the emperor — this let the Guptas control a huge area without governing it all directly.

Case 4 — Rights in action (Constitution)

Ravi, aged 12, stopped going to school to work at a roadside tea stall for long hours to support his family. A local volunteer group reported it, and officials enrolled him in a nearby government school, where he now gets free education and a mid-day meal. His friend Meena was told she could not join the school cricket team "because she is a girl". After her parents complained, the school changed its rule.
1. Which Fundamental Rights protect Ravi?

The Right against Exploitation (no child labour under 14) and the Right to Freedom, which includes free and compulsory education for ages 6–14.

2. The mid-day meal is linked to which part of the Constitution?

The Directive Principles of State Policy (welfare of children, nutrition and education).

3. Which right and which Preamble value were denied to Meena?

The Right to Equality (no discrimination on the basis of sex); the Preamble's value of equality of status and opportunity.

4. If the school had refused to change, what could Meena's family do?

Use the Right to Constitutional Remedies: approach the High Court or Supreme Court to protect her right.

5. Which Fundamental Duty did the volunteer group show?

Promoting harmony and protecting the dignity of others / helping children get education — responsible citizenship.

🌍 Enrichment: Junior Climate Impact Analyst (SDG 11 & 13)

Your role: a Junior Climate Impact Analyst for the United Nations. Your task: choose ONE real climate event, investigate the science behind it, its impact on people and the environment, and recommend solutions linked to the SDGs. Present it as a digital report, poster, presentation or documentary (8–10 slides/pages) in your SST notebook.

SDGGoalLink to your project
SDG 13Climate ActionReduce greenhouse gases (mitigation) and prepare for climate impacts (adaptation, early warnings)
SDG 11Sustainable Cities and CommunitiesSafe, resilient cities: drainage, green spaces, heat-safe buildings, disaster planning

Suggested structure (10 slides/pages)

  1. Title, your name, the event and a striking photo
  2. Where and when (map)
  3. What happened — key facts and real data (rainfall, temperature, people affected)
  4. The science: what caused it (weather + climate change link)
  5. Impact on people (lives, homes, health, jobs)
  6. Impact on the environment and economy
  7. How people and governments responded
  8. Your recommendations linked to SDG 11 and 13 (mitigation + adaptation)
  9. What young people can do
  10. Sources / bibliography
Where to find real data: UAE National Centre of Meteorology (ncm.gov.ae) • India Meteorological Department (mausam.imd.gov.in) • World Meteorological Organization (wmo.int) • NASA Climate (climate.nasa.gov) • National Snow and Ice Data Center (nsidc.org) for the Arctic • UN SDGs (sdgs.un.org) • ReliefWeb • World Weather Attribution. Always double-check numbers in at least one of these and list your sources.

📂 Fact sheets — pick one

🇦🇪 Dubai / UAE floods — April 2024
  • What: on 16 April 2024 the UAE had its heaviest rainfall since records began in 1949. Khatm Al Shakla (Al Ain) recorded about 255 mm in less than 24 hours; Dubai got more than a year's normal rain (Dubai's average is roughly 100 mm a year) in a single day.
  • Impact: roads and neighbourhoods flooded, Dubai International Airport cancelled and diverted hundreds of flights, schools moved online, homes and cars damaged; a few lives were lost in the UAE and many more in neighbouring Oman.
  • Science: a slow-moving low-pressure system pulled moist air over the Gulf. Scientists say warmer air holds more moisture, making such downpours heavier. Cities built for a desert climate have limited drainage, so water had nowhere to go.
  • Responses & solutions: the UAE announced billions of dirhams to repair homes and upgrade drainage (e.g. Dubai's "Tasreef" stormwater project); better early warnings and work-from-home orders; more green spaces and permeable surfaces (SDG 11).
🇪🇺 Europe heatwaves (Spain, Italy, Greece)
  • What: repeated record heat. Europe's highest temperature, 48.8 °C, was recorded in Sicily, Italy (August 2021); the UK passed 40 °C for the first time in July 2022; Greece faced huge wildfires (e.g. Rhodes evacuations in July 2023).
  • Impact: scientists estimate the summer of 2022 alone caused over 60,000 heat-related deaths in Europe; wildfires, droughts, crop losses, rivers too low for shipping, stress on hospitals and electricity.
  • Science: high-pressure "heat domes" trap hot air; Europe is warming faster than the global average.
  • Solutions: heat action plans and cooling centres, more trees and shade in cities, cool roofs, fire management, cutting emissions with renewables.
🇵🇰 Pakistan floods (2022)
  • What: extreme monsoon rain from June to August 2022 (Sindh and Balochistan got several times their normal rainfall), plus melting glaciers in the north.
  • Impact: about one-third of the country was under water; around 1,700 people died and about 33 million were affected; homes, crops, livestock, roads and schools destroyed; damage and losses of about US$30 billion.
  • Science: a warmer climate made the extreme rainfall heavier (World Weather Attribution); Pakistan produces less than 1% of global emissions but suffers heavily — a key example of climate injustice.
  • Solutions: flood early-warning systems, raised houses and embankments, better land use, international climate finance ("loss and damage" fund agreed at COP27, 2022).
🌍 African Sahel drought (Chad, Niger, Sudan)
  • What: the Sahel is a semi-arid belt just south of the Sahara. Rainfall is low and very unreliable; severe droughts struck in the 1970s–80s and continue.
  • Impact: crop failure, hunger, loss of livestock, people forced to migrate, conflict over land and water. Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s.
  • Science: rising temperatures increase evaporation; erratic rains; overgrazing and cutting trees cause desertification (land turning into desert).
  • Solutions: the Great Green Wall — an African-led project to restore land and plant trees across the Sahel; water harvesting, drought-resistant crops, sustainable grazing.
🇲🇻 Maldives — sea-level rise
  • What: the Maldives is the world's lowest-lying country; about 80% of its land is less than 1 m above sea level.
  • Impact: rising seas cause coastal erosion, flooding and salt water entering drinking water; warmer seas cause coral bleaching, harming fishing and tourism. In 2009 its cabinet held an underwater meeting to warn the world.
  • Science: sea levels rise because ice sheets and glaciers melt and warmer water expands.
  • Solutions: sea walls (around Malé), the raised artificial island Hulhumalé, coral reef and mangrove protection, global emission cuts.
🧊 Arctic ice melt
  • What: the Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average. Summer sea ice has shrunk sharply since satellite records began in 1979; the record low was in September 2012.
  • Impact: polar bears and seals lose their hunting platform; Indigenous communities' way of life is threatened; Greenland's melting ice raises sea levels worldwide; weather patterns may change further south.
  • Science: albedo feedback — white ice reflects sunlight, but dark ocean water absorbs it, causing even more warming and melting.
  • Solutions: only global emission cuts can slow it (Paris Agreement); protect Arctic ecosystems; monitor with satellites (NSIDC data).
🇮🇳 North India heatwaves (Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan)
  • What: in May–June 2024 a long heatwave gripped north India; Churu (Rajasthan) reached about 50.5 °C and Delhi crossed 45 °C on many days, with very warm nights.
  • Impact: many heatstroke cases and deaths (including election workers on duty), water shortages, record electricity demand and power cuts, outdoor workers and the poor hit hardest.
  • Science: hot, dry winds (loo), delayed monsoon, and global warming making heatwaves hotter and longer; concrete cities trap heat (urban heat island).
  • Solutions: city heat action plans (first in Ahmedabad, 2013), cool/white roofs, more trees and water bodies, shaded rest areas and water for workers, changing work hours, early IMD heat warnings.
Recommendations checklist: at least one mitigation idea (cut emissions), one adaptation/resilience idea (prepare and protect), one SDG 11 city idea, and one thing students can do. Explain how each one helps.
